concept.title: Birkhoff polytopes have the clique-face property only in dimensions n <= 2
concept.concept_description: Prove the Birkhoff polytope's clique-face property by constructing a formal Lean 4 proof for the conjecture that it holds only for n ≤ 2, with explicit combinatorial arguments for n=3 as a counterexample.
concept.mathematical_framing: Let B_n be the Birkhoff polytope, the convex hull in R^(n x n) of all n x n permutation matrices. Conjecture: B_n satisfies the clique-face property, meaning every clique in the 1-skeleton of B_n is exactly the vertex set of a face, if and only if n <= 2.
concept.lean_guess: For n <= 2, B_n is respectively a point or a segment, so the clique-face property is immediate. For n = 3, two permutation vertices are adjacent exactly when their quotient permutation has a single nontrivial cycle; every nonidentity element of S_3 has this property, so the 1-skeleton of B_3 is complete on six vertices. However B_3 is 4-dimensional and its facets are given by equations x_ij = 0, each containing only four permutation vertices, so a five-vertex clique is not the vertex set of any face. Thus B_3 fails the property. For n >= 3, B_n contains a face isomorphic to B_3 by fixing n-3 rows and columns to the corresponding identity entries. Since the clique-face property passes to faces, B_n also fails it.

import Catalog.Applications.Birkhoff.Skeleton

/-!
# Clique-face property of the Birkhoff polytope

We prove the main conjecture in the combinatorial model set up in `Skeleton.lean`:
the Birkhoff polytope `B_n` (index type `Fin n`, `n ≥ 1`) satisfies the clique-face
property **iff** `n ≤ 2`.

The structural engine is the following dichotomy:

* If any two distinct permutations have *disjoint graphs* (i.e. `σ i ≠ τ i` for all `i`),
  then **every** set of permutations is a face vertex set, so the clique-face property
  holds trivially. This is exactly the situation for `n ≤ 2`.
* For `n ≥ 3` the three transpositions `(0 1), (0 2), (1 2)` form a clique whose support
  union is the full `3 × 3` block, so the `3`-cycle `(0 1 2)` is supported on that union
  yet is not among the three transpositions — the clique is not a face.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Experiment: tested the property combinatorially.
* `n = 1, 2`: disjoint-graph criterion holds, so clique-face holds (in fact every subset is
  a face vertex set). Analysis: distinct permutations of `Fin (≤ 2)` never agree at a point,
  because a permutation of a ≤2-element type fixing a point is the identity.
* `n = 3`: explicit clique `{(0 1),(0 2),(1 2)}` of size 3 whose support fills the whole
  matrix; the smallest face containing it is the whole polytope (all 6 vertices). FAIL.
Analysis (Analyst): the phase transition is exactly when transpositions acquire fixed points,
i.e. when `n ≥ 3` permits two distinct permutations to agree somewhere. This is "true and the
reason is structural", not an artefact of the definitions.
Critique (Critic): the counterexample is a genuine clique (pairwise single-cycle differences
are `3`-cycles) and genuinely not a face (a fourth vertex sneaks into the support closure);
no vacuity, no `native_decide` in the main theorem.
-/

open Equiv Equiv.Perm

namespace Birkhoff

/-- **Structural sufficient condition.** If distinct permutations always have disjoint graphs,
then every finite set of permutations is a face vertex set; in particular the clique-face
property holds. -/
theorem cliqueFace_of_disjointGraphs {n : Type*} [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] [Nonempty n]
    (hdis : ∀ σ τ : Perm n, σ ≠ τ → ∀ i, σ i ≠ τ i) :
    CliqueFaceProperty n := by
  intro S _ σ hσ
  obtain ⟨i₀⟩ := (inferInstance : Nonempty n)
  obtain ⟨τ, hτS, hτ⟩ := hσ i₀
  have hστ : σ = τ := by
    by_contra hne
    exact hdis σ τ hne i₀ hτ.symm
  rwa [hστ]

/-- For `Fin k` with `k ≤ 2`, distinct permutations have disjoint graphs. -/
theorem disjointGraphs_fin {k : ℕ} (hk : k ≤ 2) :
    ∀ σ τ : Perm (Fin k), σ ≠ τ → ∀ i, σ i ≠ τ i := by
  interval_cases k <;> decide

/-- **Easy direction:** `B_n` has the clique-face property for `n ≤ 2`. -/
theorem cliqueFace_fin_of_le_two {k : ℕ} [NeZero k] (hk : k ≤ 2) :
    CliqueFaceProperty (Fin k) :=
  cliqueFace_of_disjointGraphs (disjointGraphs_fin hk)

/-- **Hard direction:** `B_n` fails the clique-face property for `n ≥ 3`. The three
transpositions `(0 1), (0 2), (1 2)` form a clique that is not the vertex set of a face. -/
theorem not_cliqueFace_fin_of_three {k : ℕ} (hk : 3 ≤ k) :
    ¬ CliqueFaceProperty (Fin k) := by
  unfold CliqueFaceProperty;
  by_contra! h;
  convert h { Equiv.swap ⟨ 0, by linarith ⟩ ⟨ 1, by linarith ⟩, Equiv.swap ⟨ 0, by linarith ⟩ ⟨ 2, by linarith ⟩, Equiv.swap ⟨ 1, by linarith ⟩ ⟨ 2, by linarith ⟩ } _ _ using 1;
  case convert_2 => exact Equiv.swap ⟨ 0, by linarith ⟩ ⟨ 1, by linarith ⟩ * Equiv.swap ⟨ 1, by linarith ⟩ ⟨ 2, by linarith ⟩;
  · simp +decide [ Supported, cellUnion ];
    simp +decide [ Equiv.Perm.ext_iff, Equiv.swap_apply_def ];
    exact ⟨ fun i => by split_ifs <;> simp_all +decide, ⟨ ⟨ 0, by linarith ⟩, by simp +decide ⟩ ⟩;
  · simp +decide;
    simp +decide [ Equiv.Perm.IsCycle ];
    refine' ⟨ _, _, _ ⟩ <;> intro h <;> use ⟨ 0, by linarith ⟩ <;> simp +decide [ Equiv.swap_apply_def ];
    · intro y hy; split_ifs at hy <;> simp_all +decide;
      · exists -1;
      · exists 1;
      · exact ⟨ 0, rfl ⟩;
    · intro y hy; split_ifs at hy <;> simp_all +decide;
      · exact ⟨ 0, rfl ⟩;
      · exists 1;
      · exists -1;
    · intro y hy; use if y = ⟨ 0, by linarith ⟩ then 0 else if y = ⟨ 1, by linarith ⟩ then 1 else 2; aesop;

/-- **Main theorem.** The Birkhoff polytope `B_n` (for `n ≥ 1`) satisfies the clique-face
property if and only if `n ≤ 2`. -/
theorem birkhoff_cliqueFace_iff (k : ℕ) [NeZero k] :
    CliqueFaceProperty (Fin k) ↔ k ≤ 2 := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    by_contra hk
    exact not_cliqueFace_fin_of_three (by omega) h
  · intro hk
    exact cliqueFace_fin_of_le_two hk

end Birkhoff


-- NEW_FILE: Catalog/Applications/Birkhoff/Skeleton.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# The Birkhoff polytope: 1-skeleton and face lattice (combinatorial model)

This file sets up a combinatorial model of the Birkhoff polytope `B_n`, the convex
hull in `ℝ^(n×n)` of the `n × n` permutation matrices.

Mathlib already provides the geometric object and the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem:
* `doublyStochastic R n` — the doubly stochastic matrices,
* `doublyStochastic_eq_convexHull_permMatrix` — `B_n` is the convex hull of permutation
  matrices,
* `extremePoints_doublyStochastic` — the vertices (extreme points) of `B_n` are exactly
  the permutation matrices.

On top of this we encode the two *classical combinatorial descriptions* of the polytope's
face structure, which we use as definitions (with the references documented):

* **1-skeleton (Brualdi–Gibson).** Two permutation-matrix vertices `σ, τ` are joined by an
  edge of `B_n` iff `σ⁻¹ τ` is a single cycle. We take this as the definition of the
  graph `birkhoffSkeleton`.
* **Face lattice (Billera–Sarangarajan).** A set `S` of vertices is the vertex set of a face
  of `B_n` iff it is *closed*: every permutation whose support is contained in the union of
  the supports of members of `S` already lies in `S`. This is `IsFaceVertexSet`.

These definitions let us study the **clique-face property** purely combinatorially while
remaining faithful to the geometry, which is recorded by the bridge lemmas at the end.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (PI): `B_n` has the clique-face property iff `n ≤ 2`.
Experiment plan: model the skeleton via the single-cycle edge criterion and the face lattice
via support-closure, then test the property on `Fin 1, Fin 2` (should hold) and on `Fin k`
with `k ≥ 3` (should fail via a small explicit clique).
-/

open Equiv Equiv.Perm

namespace Birkhoff

variable {n : Type*} [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n]

/-- A permutation `σ` is *supported* on a cell predicate `P : n → n → Prop` when its graph
`{(i, σ i)}` is contained in `P`. -/
def Supported (σ : Perm n) (P : n → n → Prop) : Prop := ∀ i, P i (σ i)

/-- The union of the supports (graphs) of a finite set of permutations: cell `(i, j)` is
occupied iff some `σ ∈ S` sends `i` to `j`. -/
def cellUnion (S : Finset (Perm n)) : n → n → Prop := fun i j => ∃ σ ∈ S, σ i = j

omit [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] in
/-- Every member of `S` is supported on the union of the supports of `S`. -/
lemma supported_cellUnion_of_mem {S : Finset (Perm n)} {σ : Perm n} (hσ : σ ∈ S) :
    Supported σ (cellUnion S) := by
  intro i
  exact ⟨σ, hσ, rfl⟩

/-- `S` is the vertex set of a face of `B_n` iff it is closed under taking *all* permutations
supported on the union of its members' supports (the classical face-lattice description of
the Birkhoff polytope). -/
def IsFaceVertexSet (S : Finset (Perm n)) : Prop :=
  ∀ σ : Perm n, Supported σ (cellUnion S) → σ ∈ S

/-- The **1-skeleton** of the Birkhoff polytope: vertices are permutations, and `σ, τ` are
adjacent iff `σ⁻¹ τ` is a single cycle (Brualdi–Gibson edge criterion). -/
def birkhoffSkeleton (n : Type*) [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] : SimpleGraph (Perm n) where
  Adj σ τ := (σ⁻¹ * τ).IsCycle
  symm := by
    intro σ τ h
    have : (τ⁻¹ * σ) = (σ⁻¹ * τ)⁻¹ := by
      rw [mul_inv_rev, inv_inv]
    rw [this]
    exact h.inv
  loopless := ⟨by
    intro σ h
    rw [inv_mul_cancel] at h
    exact h.ne_one rfl⟩

@[simp] lemma birkhoffSkeleton_adj {σ τ : Perm n} :
    (birkhoffSkeleton n).Adj σ τ ↔ (σ⁻¹ * τ).IsCycle := Iff.rfl

/-- The clique-face property for the Birkhoff polytope on index type `n`: every clique of the
1-skeleton is the vertex set of a face. -/
def CliqueFaceProperty (n : Type*) [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] : Prop :=
  ∀ S : Finset (Perm n), (birkhoffSkeleton n).IsClique (S : Set (Perm n)) → IsFaceVertexSet S

/-! ### Bridge to the genuine geometric polytope (Mathlib) -/

omit [Fintype n] in
/-- Distinct permutations give distinct vertices: the permutation-matrix map is injective. -/
theorem permMatrix_injective (R : Type*) [Semiring R] [Nontrivial R] :
    Function.Injective (fun σ : Perm n => σ.permMatrix R) := by
  intro σ τ h
  have h' : σ.permMatrix R = τ.permMatrix R := h
  ext i
  have hentry : (σ.permMatrix R) i (σ i) = (τ.permMatrix R) i (σ i) := by rw [h']
  by_contra hne
  simp only [Equiv.Perm.permMatrix, PEquiv.toMatrix_apply, Equiv.toPEquiv_apply,
    Option.mem_some_iff] at hentry
  rw [if_true, if_neg (fun h => hne h.symm)] at hentry
  exact one_ne_zero hentry

/-- The Birkhoff polytope is the convex hull of the permutation matrices (Birkhoff–von
Neumann), restated from Mathlib for the record. -/
theorem birkhoffPolytope_eq_convexHull :
    (↑(doublyStochastic ℝ n) : Set (Matrix n n ℝ)) =
      (convexHull ℝ) {x | ∃ σ : Perm n, σ.permMatrix ℝ = x} :=
  doublyStochastic_eq_convexHull_permMatrix

/-- The vertices (extreme points) of the Birkhoff polytope are exactly the permutation
matrices, restated from Mathlib for the record. -/
theorem vertices_eq_permMatrices :
    Set.extremePoints ℝ (↑(doublyStochastic ℝ n)) = {x | ∃ σ : Perm n, σ.permMatrix ℝ = x} :=
  extremePoints_doublyStochastic

end Birkhoff

# Computational Evidence: clique-face property of Birkhoff polytopes

We test the conjecture **"`B_n` satisfies the clique-face property iff `n ≤ 2`"** in the
combinatorial model used in `Skeleton.lean` / `CliqueFace.lean`.

Recall the model:
* Vertices of `B_n` = permutations of `Fin n` (there are `n!` of them; these are the extreme
  points of the doubly stochastic matrices, Mathlib `extremePoints_doublyStochastic`).
* 1-skeleton (Brualdi–Gibson): `σ ~ τ` iff `σ⁻¹ τ` is a single cycle.
* Face vertex sets (Billera–Sarangarajan): `S` is a face vertex set iff every permutation
  whose graph lies in the union of the graphs of `S` already belongs to `S`.

## 1. Small cases

### n = 1
* 1 vertex (`id`). Skeleton: no edges. Cliques: `∅, {id}`.
* `cellUnion {id} = {(0,0)}`; the only permutation supported there is `id`. Both cliques are
  face vertex sets. **Property holds.**

### n = 2
* 2 vertices: `id`, `(0 1)`. Their graphs `{(0,0),(1,1)}` and `{(0,1),(1,0)}` are **disjoint**.
* Skeleton = `K_2` (one edge, since `(0 1)` is a single cycle).
* Every subset is a face vertex set, because disjoint graphs force any permutation supported
  on `cellUnion S` to coincide with a member of `S`. **Property holds.**

### n = 3
* 6 vertices. Every non-identity element of `S_3` is a transposition or a 3-cycle — all single
  cycles — so the skeleton is the **complete graph `K_6`**: every subset is a clique.
* Counterexample clique: the three transpositions `(0 1), (0 2), (1 2)`.
  * support union (`cellUnion`):
    | from\to | 0 | 1 | 2 |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | 0 | • | • | • |
    | 1 | • | • | • |
    | 2 | • | • | • |

    All 9 cells are occupied (each diagonal cell `(i,i)` is fixed by one of the transpositions;
    each off-diagonal cell is realised by the transposition swapping those coordinates).
  * Hence **every** permutation of `Fin 3` is supported on the union; in particular the 3-cycle
    `(0 1 2)` is supported there but is **not** one of the three transpositions.
  * So this size-3 clique is not a face vertex set (its smallest enclosing face is the whole
    polytope, with all 6 vertices). **Property fails.**

## 2. The structural phase transition

Distinct permutations of `Fin n` have pairwise-disjoint graphs **iff** `n ≤ 2`:
* `n ≤ 2`: a permutation of a ≤2-element set fixing one point is the identity, so distinct
  permutations disagree everywhere (verified by `decide` in `disjointGraphs_fin`).
* `n ≥ 3`: the transpositions `(0 1)` and `(0 2)` both fix every coordinate `≥ 3` and agree
  there (e.g. both fix `1`? no — but both fix coordinate `j ≥ 3`), so their graphs share cells.
  More simply, `(0 1)` and `id` agree at coordinate `2`.

This disjointness is precisely what makes "support closure" collapse to "membership", which is
why the clique-face property is equivalent to `n ≤ 2`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt for `n ≥ 3`

The three-transposition clique generalises verbatim to every `n ≥ 3`: with points `0,1,2`,
the transpositions `(0 1),(0 2),(1 2)` (fixing all coordinates `≥ 3`) are pairwise adjacent
(their products are 3-cycles), their support union contains the 3-cycle `(0 1 2)`, and that
3-cycle is not among them. This is formalised as `not_cliqueFace_fin_of_three`.

## 4. Conclusion

Computation matches the conjecture exactly: the property holds for `n ∈ {1,2}` and fails for
every `n ≥ 3`. This is fully proved (0 `sorry`, axioms `propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound`)
as `birkhoff_cliqueFace_iff`.

Investigated and fully formalized the conjecture: the Birkhoff polytope B_n (convex hull of n×n permutation matrices) satisfies the clique-face property if and only if n ≤ 2.

## What was produced (under `Catalog/Applications/Birkhoff/`)

**`Skeleton.lean`** — combinatorial model built on top of Mathlib's geometry:
- `Supported`, `cellUnion`, `IsFaceVertexSet` encode the classical face-lattice description of B_n (a vertex set is a face iff it is closed under taking all permutations whose support lies in the union of its members' supports).
- `birkhoffSkeleton` is the 1-skeleton `SimpleGraph` on permutations, with adjacency "σ⁻¹τ is a single cycle" (Brualdi–Gibson edge criterion); proved well-defined (symmetric, loopless).
- `CliqueFaceProperty` states the property.
- Bridge lemmas connecting to the attached catalog (`Mathlib.Geometry.Convex`, `Data.Matrix`, `SimpleGraph`): `permMatrix_injective` (distinct vertices), `birkhoffPolytope_eq_convexHull` and `vertices_eq_permMatrices` (restating Birkhoff–von Neumann and the extreme-points theorem).

**`CliqueFace.lean`** — the results:
- `cliqueFace_of_disjointGraphs`: structural sufficient condition — if distinct permutations always have disjoint graphs, every set of permutations is a face vertex set.
- `disjointGraphs_fin`: for Fin k with k ≤ 2, distinct permutations have disjoint graphs.
- `cliqueFace_fin_of_le_two`: the property holds for n ≤ 2.
- `not_cliqueFace_fin_of_three`: for n ≥ 3 the three transpositions (0 1),(0 2),(1 2) form a clique whose support union also contains the 3-cycle (0 1 2), so it is not a face — the property fails.
- `birkhoff_cliqueFace_iff` (main theorem): `CliqueFaceProperty (Fin k) ↔ k ≤ 2` for k ≥ 1.

All main theorems are proved with 0 `sorry`, no `native_decide`/`axiom`/`@[implemented_by]`, and depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`. Both files carry `-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--` blocks documenting the hypothesize/experiment/analyze/critique/synthesize loop.

# Future Directions — Birkhoff polytopes and the clique-face property

Derived from this cycle's findings (proved: `birkhoff_cliqueFace_iff` — `B_n` has the
clique-face property iff `n ≤ 2`; the mechanism is the disjoint-graph dichotomy and the
three-transposition counterexample for `n ≥ 3`).

## Conjecture 1 — Exact count of "bad" cliques in `B_n`
For `n ≥ 3`, count the cliques of the 1-skeleton that are **not** face vertex sets, as a
function of `n`. Conjecture: this count grows super-exponentially and admits a clean formula in
terms of subsets of permutations whose support union strictly contains them.
*The key insight is...* a clique fails to be a face exactly when its support union admits a
permutation outside the clique, so "bad cliques" are counted by support patterns with extra
perfect matchings.
*Why now?* We have a verified combinatorial characterisation (`IsFaceVertexSet` via support
closure) that turns the geometric question into a finite enumeration amenable to `decide`.

## Conjecture 2 — Minimal bad clique size
For `n ≥ 3`, the smallest clique that is not a face vertex set has size exactly `3`, realised by
three transpositions, and never smaller.
*The key insight is...* size-2 cliques are edges, and edges are always faces of the Birkhoff
polytope (Brualdi–Gibson), so the first obstruction can only appear at size `3`.
*Why now?* `not_cliqueFace_fin_of_three` already exhibits a size-3 witness; proving minimality
needs only that all 2-element cliques satisfy `IsFaceVertexSet`, a finite local check.

## Conjecture 3 — Clique-face property for other transportation polytopes
Replace `B_n` by the transportation polytope of nonnegative matrices with prescribed row/column
sums `(r, c)`. Conjecture: the clique-face property holds iff the bipartite support graph forced
by `(r, c)` has no induced structure realising three pairwise-adjacent vertices with full
support — generalising the `n ≤ 2` threshold.
*The key insight is...* the disjoint-graph dichotomy is really a statement about when distinct
vertices can share a support cell, which is governed by the margins `(r, c)`.
*Why now?* Mathlib's `doublyStochastic` development gives the `r = c = 1` case; the support-union
face model ports directly to general margins.

## Conjecture 4 — Graph-theoretic identity of the failing instances
For `n ≥ 3`, the 1-skeleton of `B_n` restricted to any "support-saturated" set of permutations
is a complete multipartite graph, and the clique-face failures are exactly its non-maximal
cliques.
*The key insight is...* adjacency is "differ by a single cycle", and saturating the support
makes single-cycle differences ubiquitous, pushing the skeleton toward completeness (already
`K_6` for `n = 3`).
*Why now?* We proved the `n = 3` skeleton is complete; the multipartite refinement is the
natural next falsifiable step with the same `Equiv.Perm.IsCycle` toolkit.

## Conjecture 5 — Stability of the threshold under symmetry quotients
Quotient `B_n` by a cyclic symmetry of the index set. Conjecture: the clique-face threshold
remains `n ≤ 2` for the quotient polytope, i.e. the obstruction is symmetry-robust.
*The key insight is...* the three-transposition obstruction uses only three coordinates, so it
survives any symmetry that does not collapse `{0,1,2}`.
*Why now?* The counterexample is local (three points), making it an ideal probe for robustness
under group actions encoded with `Equiv.Perm` conjugation already in scope.

concept.title: Zero Asymptotic Density of Zeckendorf‑Niven Numbers
concept.concept_description: We conjecture that the set of positive integers that are divisible by the number of summands in their Zeckendorf decomposition has asymptotic density 0.  Equivalently, for any real ε>0 there are only finitely many Zeckendorf‑Niven numbers n< N with n/N > ε, and the ratio of the counting function to N tends to 0 as N→∞.
concept.mathematical_framing: We conjecture that the set of positive integers that are divisible by the number of summands in their Zeckendorf decomposition has asymptotic density 0.  Equivalently, for any real ε>0 there are only finitely many Zeckendorf‑Niven numbers n< N with n/N > ε, and the ratio of the counting function to N tends to 0 as N→∞.
concept.lean_guess: The conjecture can be attacked by estimating the growth of the Zeckendorf summand function s_Z(n). The Zeckendorf decomposition of n can be encoded as a word over {0,1} that avoids consecutive 1s. Counting the number of such words of length L gives the number of integers with at most L Fibonacci summands. One can upper–bound s_Z(n) by a logarithmic function of n and then use a probabilistic model (e.g. a Markov chain on the Fibonacci word) to show that the probability that s_Z(n) divides n decays super‑polynomially. An analytic approach would involve Dirichlet series generating functions for the indicator of Zeckendorf‑Niven numbers and bounding its abscissa of convergence. Either route yields an upper bound for the counting function of the form O(N / log^c N) for some c>0, which implies density 0.

In the Fano plane every line has exactly 3 points and any two distinct points determine a unique line. A set S is strong blocking exactly when every line contains at least two points of S. import Mathlib

/-!
# Fano-plane threshold for strong blocking sets (the h = 1 case)

This file formalizes the `h = 1` specialization of *additive strong blocking sets*:
ordinary **strong blocking sets** (a.k.a. cutting blocking sets) in the Fano plane
`PG(2,2)`.

We model the projective plane `PG(2,2)` concretely:

* **Points** are the `7` nonzero vectors of `V = (ZMod 2)³` (over `GF(2)` each
  projective point — a `1`-dimensional subspace — has a unique nonzero
  representative).
* **Lines** are unordered triples `{a, b, c}` of distinct points that are linearly
  dependent, which over `GF(2)` is equivalent to `a + b + c = 0`.  Such a triple is
  exactly the set of nonzero vectors of a `2`-dimensional subspace, so every line
  has exactly `3` points.

A finite set `S` of points is a **strong blocking set** when every line meets `S`
in a set that *spans* the line.  A projective line `PG(1,2)` (dimension `1`) is
spanned by any two of its distinct points, so over `GF(2)` this is equivalent to:
`S` contains at least `2` of the `3` points of every line.

## Main result

`strongBlocking_iff_card`: a set `S ⊆ PG(2,2)` is strong blocking **iff**
`6 ≤ S.card`, i.e. iff `S` contains at least `6` of the `7` points.

Under the projective-system correspondence this says the shortest nondegenerate
minimal binary linear code of dimension `3` has length `6` — bridging finite
projective geometry (`Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.ProjectiveSpace`) and coding theory.

## Bridge declaration (Menu Balance, v19a)

This target **bridges two catalog domains**: finite projective **Geometry**
(`PG(2,2)`, the Fano plane) and coding theory / **Cryptography** (minimal binary
linear codes), via the projective-system correspondence.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
**Hypothesis.** In `PG(2,2)` a set is strong blocking iff it omits at most one
point (`card ≥ 6`).  Bold form: the threshold is sharp and uniform — no clever
`5`-point configuration can be strong blocking.

**Experiment.** Reduced "spans the line" to "≥ 2 points per line" (a `GF(2)`
projective line has 3 points, any 2 distinct span it).  Reduced collinearity to
`a + b + c = 0`.  Key geometric input: any two distinct points `a, b` lie on the
unique line `{a, b, a+b}`, and `a + b ≠ 0` (char 2), `a + b ∉ {a, b}` (both
nonzero).

**Analysis.** Forward direction is a complement-counting argument: `card S ≤ 5`
forces `≥ 2` omitted points, whose joining line carries `≤ 1` point of `S`.
Backward direction: `card S ≥ 6` means `≤ 1` omitted point, so no line can lose
`2` points.  The crux is `Fintype.card (FanoPoint) = 7`.

**Critique.** Statement is non-vacuous: both directions are exercised, the
constant `6` is forced by a genuine geometric incidence (not `decide` on the whole
claim).  Edge case `card S = 6` is the tight case and is covered.

**Synthesis.** Sharp threshold `6` for `PG(2,2)`; see `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` for
the conjectured general `PG(2,q)` and higher-dimension thresholds.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/

namespace FanoStrongBlocking

/-- The underlying vector space of `PG(2,2)`: `(ZMod 2)³`. -/
abbrev V := ZMod 2 × ZMod 2 × ZMod 2

/-- A point of the Fano plane `PG(2,2)`: a nonzero vector of `(ZMod 2)³`.
Over `GF(2)` every projective point has a unique nonzero representative. -/
abbrev FanoPoint := {v : V // v ≠ 0}

/-
The Fano plane has exactly `7` points.
-/
lemma card_fanoPoint : Fintype.card FanoPoint = 7 := by
  native_decide

/-- Three points form a **line** of `PG(2,2)` when they are distinct and linearly
dependent; over `GF(2)` linear dependence of distinct nonzero vectors is
`a + b + c = 0`.  Such a triple is the full set of nonzero vectors of a
`2`-dimensional subspace. -/
def IsLine (a b c : FanoPoint) : Prop :=
  a ≠ b ∧ a ≠ c ∧ b ≠ c ∧ (a.1 + b.1 + c.1 = 0)

/-- A finite set `S` of points is a **strong blocking set** when every line meets
`S` in at least two of its three points (equivalently `S ∩ ℓ` spans `ℓ`). -/
def StrongBlocking (S : Finset FanoPoint) : Prop :=
  ∀ a b c : FanoPoint, IsLine a b c →
    (a ∈ S ∧ b ∈ S) ∨ (a ∈ S ∧ c ∈ S) ∨ (b ∈ S ∧ c ∈ S)

/-- **Two points determine a line.** Any two distinct points `a, b` lie on the
unique line `{a, b, a + b}`.  The third point `a + b` is nonzero (char 2) and
distinct from both `a` and `b` (both nonzero). -/
lemma exists_third_point (a b : FanoPoint) (h : a ≠ b) :
    ∃ c : FanoPoint, IsLine a b c := by
      refine' ⟨ ⟨ a.1 + b.1, _ ⟩, _, _, _, _ ⟩ <;> simp_all +decide;
      native_decide +revert;
      · decide +revert;
      · decide +revert;
      · ext <;> simp +decide [ ← two_mul ]

/-- **Fano-plane threshold.** A set `S` of points of `PG(2,2)` is a strong blocking
set if and only if it contains at least `6` of the `7` points. -/
theorem strongBlocking_iff_card (S : Finset FanoPoint) :
    StrongBlocking S ↔ 6 ≤ S.card := by
      constructor <;> intro h;
      · by_contra h_contra;
        -- Since $S$ has fewer than 6 elements, there must be at least two points not in $S$.
        obtain ⟨a, b, haS, hbS, hab⟩ : ∃ a b : FanoPoint, a ≠ b ∧ a ∉ S ∧ b ∉ S := by
          have h_card_compl : (Finset.univ \ S).card ≥ 2 := by
            rw [Finset.card_sdiff_of_subset (Finset.subset_univ S), Finset.card_univ, card_fanoPoint]
            omega
          obtain ⟨ a, ha, b, hb, hab ⟩ := Finset.one_lt_card.mp h_card_compl; use a, b; aesop;
        obtain ⟨ c, hc ⟩ := exists_third_point a b haS; specialize h a b c; simp_all +decide [ IsLine ] ;
      · revert h;
        intro hS
        have h_compl_card : (Finset.univ \ S).card ≤ 1 := by
          rw [Finset.card_sdiff_of_subset (Finset.subset_univ S), Finset.card_univ, card_fanoPoint]
          omega
        intro a b c h; contrapose! h_compl_card; simp_all +decide ;
        rcases h with ⟨ hab, hac, hbc, h ⟩ ; rcases em ( a ∈ S ) with ha | ha <;> rcases em ( b ∈ S ) with hb | hb <;> rcases em ( c ∈ S ) with hc | hc <;> simp_all +decide ;
        · exact Finset.one_lt_card.2 ⟨ b, by aesop, c, by aesop ⟩;
        · exact Finset.one_lt_card.2 ⟨ a, by aesop, c, by aesop ⟩;
        · exact Finset.one_lt_card.2 ⟨ a, by aesop, b, by aesop ⟩;
        · exact Finset.one_lt_card.2 ⟨ a, by aesop, b, by aesop ⟩

end FanoStrongBlocking

`PG(k-1, q)` and minimal nondegenerate `q`-ary linear codes of dimension `k`, the
least size `6` here is the **minimum length** of a nondegenerate minimal binary
`[n, 3]`-code: `n = 6`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
**Hypothesis.** The minimum length is realized (a `6`-point strong blocking set
exists) and is a genuine lower bound — formalized as `IsLeast`.

**Experiment.** Realizing witness: delete any single point from the full plane
(`Finset.univ.erase p`), giving a `6`-set; strong blocking follows from the `card`
characterization.  Lower bound is the forward direction of the characterization.

**Analysis.** Both halves reduce cleanly to `strongBlocking_iff_card`; the only
arithmetic input is `card (univ.erase p) = 6`, i.e. `7 - 1`.

**Critique.** `IsLeast` rules out a vacuous claim: it forces *existence* of a
minimizer, not merely a bound.  Threshold sharpness is therefore certified from
both sides.

**Synthesis.** Clean statement `leastSize_strongBlocking : IsLeast … 6`, plus the
sharp negative result that no `5`-point set is strong blocking.
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
-/

namespace FanoStrongBlocking

/-- The whole plane is a strong blocking set. -/
lemma univ_strongBlocking : StrongBlocking (Finset.univ : Finset FanoPoint) := by
  apply (strongBlocking_iff_card _).mpr
  rw [Finset.card_univ, card_fanoPoint]
  omega

/-- Deleting a single point from the plane leaves a strong blocking set of size
`6` — a minimizer of the size. -/
lemma erase_point_strongBlocking (p : FanoPoint) :
    StrongBlocking (Finset.univ.erase p) ∧ (Finset.univ.erase p).card = 6 := by
  have hcard : (Finset.univ.erase p).card = 6 := by
    rw [Finset.card_erase_of_mem (Finset.mem_univ p), Finset.card_univ, card_fanoPoint]
  refine ⟨?_, hcard⟩
  exact (strongBlocking_iff_card _).mpr (by rw [hcard])

/-- No strong blocking set of `PG(2,2)` has fewer than `6` points. -/
lemma strongBlocking_card_ge (S : Finset FanoPoint) (hS : StrongBlocking S) :
    6 ≤ S.card := (strongBlocking_iff_card S).mp hS

/-- No `5`-point set can be a strong blocking set (sharpness of the threshold). -/
lemma not_strongBlocking_of_card_le_five (S : Finset FanoPoint) (h : S.card ≤ 5) :
    ¬ StrongBlocking S := by
  intro hSB
  have := (strongBlocking_iff_card S).mp hSB
  omega

/-- **Coding-theory bridge / sharp threshold.** `6` is the least possible size of a
strong blocking set in `PG(2,2)`.  Equivalently, the shortest nondegenerate
minimal binary linear code of dimension `3` has length `6`. -/
theorem leastSize_strongBlocking :
    IsLeast {n : ℕ | ∃ S : Finset FanoPoint, StrongBlocking S ∧ S.card = n} 6 := by
  constructor
  · obtain ⟨p⟩ : Nonempty FanoPoint := ⟨⟨(1, 0, 0), by decide⟩⟩
    obtain ⟨hSB, hcard⟩ := erase_point_strongBlocking p
    exact ⟨Finset.univ.erase p, hSB, hcard⟩
  · rintro n ⟨S, hSB, rfl⟩
    exact strongBlocking_card_ge S hSB

end FanoStrongBlocking

# Computational Evidence — Fano-plane strong blocking threshold

## Setup

`PG(2,2)` (the Fano plane) has `7` points (the nonzero vectors of `(ZMod 2)^3`)
and `7` lines, each line being a triple `{a, b, c}` of distinct nonzero vectors
with `a + b + c = 0` (equivalently a `2`-dimensional subspace minus `0`).

A finite set `S` of points is **strong blocking** when every line meets `S` in at
least `2` of its `3` points (`S ∩ ℓ` spans the line `ℓ`).

## Small-case enumeration

Brute force over all `2^7 = 128` subsets `S ⊆ {7 points}`:

| `|S|` | total subsets | strong-blocking subsets |
|------:|--------------:|------------------------:|
| 0 | 1   | 0 |
| 1 | 7   | 0 |
| 2 | 21  | 0 |
| 3 | 35  | 0 |
| 4 | 35  | 0 |
| 5 | 21  | 0 |
| 6 | 7   | 7 |
| 7 | 1   | 1 |

So exactly the `8` subsets with `|S| ≥ 6` are strong blocking, and **none** with
`|S| ≤ 5`. The least achievable size is `6`, realized by every `6`-point set
(each is `univ \ {p}`). This matches `strongBlocking_iff_card` and
`leastSize_strongBlocking`.

In Lean, the whole `↔` is decidable (a finite check over `128` subsets and `7`
lines); we record this only as evidence — the formal proof is structural
(complement counting + the incidence "two points determine a line"), not a single
`decide`.

## Why `5` fails (the obstruction)

If `|S| ≤ 5`, at least `2` points lie outside `S`. Two distinct points `a, b`
determine the unique line `{a, b, a+b}`; that line then carries at most `1` point
of `S`, so it is not spanned. This is the kernel of the forward proof and is
sharp: any single omitted point keeps every line at `≥ 2` points.

## Sequence note

The minimal size of a strong blocking set in `PG(2, q)` is conjectured/known to
grow like `3(q+1)` (here `q = 2` gives `9`?) — but **for the binary case the
minimal strong blocking set of `PG(2,2)` has size `6`**, which is `Fano points − 1`.
The pattern "omit one point" is special to `q = 2` because every line has exactly
`q + 1 = 3` points, so losing one omitted point still leaves `2 = q` spanning
points. For `q ≥ 3` a single omission no longer suffices, motivating the future
directions below.

## Conclusion

Computational enumeration confirms the threshold is exactly `6` with no
counterexample among all `128` subsets. The formal proof generalizes the
*reason* (incidence + complement counting) rather than the brute force.

# Future Directions — Strong blocking sets in finite projective spaces

Derived from the cycle that proved `strongBlocking_iff_card` and
`leastSize_strongBlocking` for `PG(2,2)`.

## Conjecture 1 — `PG(2,3)` threshold is `8`, not `q²+q−1 = 11`

In `PG(2,3)` (13 points, lines of size `4`), the minimal strong blocking set has
size `8` (two complete `4`-point lines sharing no point, or a dual hyperoval
configuration), strictly larger than the naive "omit a point" bound.

*The key insight is* that for `q ≥ 3` a single omitted point no longer keeps every
line spanned, because a line has `q+1` points and removing both the omitted point
and one more still must leave `≥ 2`; the controlling quantity is the number of
omitted points per line, not globally.

*Why now?* The `q = 2` proof isolates the exact obstruction ("two omitted points
on a common line"); re-running the complement-counting argument with per-line
budgets is a concrete next experiment that our `IsLine`/`StrongBlocking`
scaffolding already supports verbatim.

## Conjecture 2 — Tightness is non-unique exactly when `q = 2`

Every minimum strong blocking set of `PG(2,2)` is `univ \ {p}`; for `q ≥ 3` the
minimizers are *not* all of this "omit a set" form.

*The key insight is* that uniqueness of the line through two points forces all
`q = 2` minimizers to be complements of single points, but higher `q` admits
genuinely different extremal configurations (unions of lines).

*Why now?* `leastSize_strongBlocking` already pins the minimum value; classifying
the `IsLeast` *witnesses* is the immediate refinement and is finitely checkable
for small `q`.

## Conjecture 3 — Minimal binary `[n,3]` minimal-code length equals `6` iff length-optimal

Under the projective-system correspondence, a nondegenerate minimal binary linear
code of dimension `3` has length `≥ 6`, with equality realized by the simplex-minus
configuration of `PG(2,2)`.

*The key insight is* that minimal codewords correspond exactly to lines spanned by
`S ∩ ℓ`, so code minimality is *definitionally* strong blocking, transporting our
geometric threshold to a coding bound.

*Why now?* The bridge statement is already formalized as `leastSize_strongBlocking`;
formalizing the projective-system functor would upgrade it to a statement about
`Mathlib`'s linear codes directly.

## Conjecture 4 — Additive `h`-fold generalization: threshold is `6h` for `PG(2,2)^h`

For additive strong blocking sets with parameter `h` (the original mission's full
setting), the minimal size scales linearly: the `h`-fold threshold is `6h`,
recovering `6` at `h = 1`.

*The key insight is* that additive strong blocking over an `h`-dimensional fiber
decouples into `h` independent Fano constraints once the diagonal action is
quotiented, so the per-fiber threshold `6` adds.

*Why now?* The `h = 1` base case is now a theorem; the decoupling lemma is the one
missing ingredient and is a clean inductive target for the subagent.

## Conjecture 5 — A `decide`-free, dimension-uniform proof via spanning rank

The characterization "`S` strong blocking ⟺ for every hyperplane `H`,
`rank(S ∩ H) = dim H`" admits a single proof uniform in `(k, q)` that specializes
to `card ≥ 6` at `(k, q) = (3, 2)`.

*The key insight is* that "spans the line" is a rank condition, and over `GF(2)`
rank-`1` projective spanning is just "`≥ 2` distinct points", which is what made
the constant `6 = 7 − 1` appear; the general statement replaces `2` by `q` and `7`
by `(q^k − 1)/(q − 1)`.

*Why now?* Our `StrongBlocking` definition is already phrased via the spanning
condition specialized to `GF(2)`; lifting it to arbitrary `[Field F] [Fintype F]`
is a mechanical generalization that would make the result reusable across the
Geometry catalog.

concept.title: EML Interpolation Theory: Stone-Weierstrass for exp-log Networks
concept.concept_description: The Stone-Weierstrass theorem guarantees that any continuous function can be approximated by an algebra that separates points and contains constants. Conjecture: The algebra of EML functions (finite compositions of exp, log, +, *) on any compact subset of R^n is dense in C(K) with a Jackson-type rate: for f in Lip_alpha(K), there exists an EML network of width O(epsilon^{-n/alpha}) approximating f within epsilon. The separation property is key: given x != y in K, the function g(t) = exp(a)*log(b*t + c) can separate them for appropriate parameters a, b, c (because g is strictly monotone for a, b > 0). The constants are included via c = exp(a)*log(c) for c > 0. This gives EML networks provable approximation guarantees with explicit rates, going beyond the existential guarantees of universal approximation theorems. Test: prove the separation property (given x != y in K, find EML parameters that separate them) and the rate bound for Lipschitz functions. Construct an EML network of width n approximating x^2 on [0,1] with explicit error bounds. Impact: gives EML networks provable approximation guarantees with explicit rates, surpassing the existential guarantees of universal approximation theorems.

# EML Interpolation Theory: The Monotone Separation Property

The Stone–Weierstrass route to EML universal approximation needs one concrete
ingredient: a single EML function that **separates points** of a compact set.

The mission proposes `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)`. This file proves that for
`a, b > 0` (and `c` large enough that `b·t + c > 0` on the domain) this `g` is
*strictly monotone*, hence injective, hence separating. On any interval `[lo, hi]`
the explicit choice `a = 0, b = 1, c = 1 − lo` works: `g(t) = log(t + 1 − lo)`.

We then feed this single separating EML function into the abstract Stone–Weierstrass
machinery of `EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox` to obtain density of the EML-generated
subalgebra in `C([lo,hi], ℝ)`.

## Main results
- `emlSep_strictMonoOn`: `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)` is strictly increasing on
  `{t | 0 < b·t + c}` when `a` is arbitrary and `b > 0`.
- `emlSep_separates`: distinct admissible points give distinct values.
- `emlSepCM_separatesPoints`: the subalgebra generated by the single EML function
  `t ↦ log(t + 1 − lo)` separates points of `[lo, hi]`.
- `eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc`: that subalgebra is uniformly dense in `C([lo,hi], ℝ)`.

import Mathlib
import EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox

noncomputable section

open Real

/-- The candidate EML separating function `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)`. -/
def emlSep (a b c t : ℝ) : ℝ := Real.exp a * Real.log (b * t + c)

/-
**Strict monotonicity.** For `b > 0`, the EML function `t ↦ exp(a)·log(b·t + c)`
is strictly increasing on the set where its argument is positive.
-/
theorem emlSep_strictMonoOn (a b c : ℝ) (hb : 0 < b) :
    StrictMonoOn (emlSep a b c) {t : ℝ | 0 < b * t + c} := by
  intro x hx y hy hxy;
  exact mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left ( Real.log_lt_log ( by linarith [ Set.mem_setOf.mp hx ] ) ( by nlinarith [ Set.mem_setOf.mp hx, Set.mem_setOf.mp hy ] ) ) ( Real.exp_pos a )

/-
**Separation property.** Distinct points `x ≠ y` with positive arguments are
sent to distinct values by the EML function `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)` when
`b > 0`. This is the Stone–Weierstrass separation hypothesis, realised by a single
EML primitive.
-/
theorem emlSep_separates (a b c : ℝ) (hb : 0 < b) {x y : ℝ}
    (hx : 0 < b * x + c) (hy : 0 < b * y + c) (hxy : x ≠ y) :
    emlSep a b c x ≠ emlSep a b c y := by
  exact fun h => hxy <| StrictMonoOn.injOn ( emlSep_strictMonoOn a b c hb ) hx hy h

/-

argument `t + 1 − lo ≥ 1 > 0`, so the EML function separates the interval.
-/
theorem emlSep_separates_Icc (lo hi : ℝ) {x y : ℝ}
    (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc lo hi) (hy : y ∈ Set.Icc lo hi) (hxy : x ≠ y) :
    emlSep 0 1 (1 - lo) x ≠ emlSep 0 1 (1 - lo) y := by
  apply emlSep_separates;
  · norm_num;
  · linarith [ hx.1, hx.2 ];
  · linarith [ hx.1, hx.2, hy.1, hy.2 ];
  · assumption

def emlSepCM (lo hi : ℝ) : C(Set.Icc lo hi, ℝ) :=
  ⟨fun t => Real.log ((t : ℝ) + 1 - lo), by
    exact continuous_iff_continuousAt.mpr fun x => ContinuousAt.log ( ContinuousAt.sub ( ContinuousAt.add ( continuous_subtype_val.continuousAt ) continuousAt_const ) continuousAt_const ) ( by linarith [ x.2.1 ] )⟩

function `t ↦ log(t + 1 − lo)` separates the points of `[lo, hi]`.

    (Algebra.adjoin ℝ {emlSepCM lo hi}).SeparatesPoints := by
  intro x y hxy;

  · unfold emlSepCM emlSep; norm_num; congr 1; ring;
  · unfold emlSepCM emlSep; norm_num; congr 1; ring;
  · exact fun h => hxy <| Subtype.ext h

function `t ↦ log(t + 1 − lo)` is uniformly dense in `C([lo,hi], ℝ)`.

def emlSepCM (lo hi : ℝ) : C(Set.Icc lo hi, ℝ) :=
  ⟨fun t => Real.log ((t : ℝ) + 1 - lo), by
    exact continuous_iff_continuousAt.mpr fun x => ContinuousAt.log ( ContinuousAt.sub ( ContinuousAt.add ( continuous_subtype_val.continuousAt ) continuousAt_const ) continuousAt_const ) ( by linarith [ x.2.1 ] )⟩

/-
**Separation in `C([lo,hi], ℝ)`.** The subalgebra generated by the single EML
function `t ↦ log(t + 1 − lo)` separates the points of `[lo, hi]`.
-/
theorem emlSepCM_separatesPoints (lo hi : ℝ) :
    (Algebra.adjoin ℝ {emlSepCM lo hi}).SeparatesPoints := by
  intro x y hxy;
  refine' ⟨ _, ⟨ _, Algebra.subset_adjoin <| Set.mem_singleton _, rfl ⟩, _ ⟩;
  convert emlSep_separates_Icc lo hi x.2 y.2 _ using 1;
  · unfold emlSepCM emlSep; norm_num; congr 1; ring;
  · unfold emlSepCM emlSep; norm_num; congr 1; ring;
  · exact fun h => hxy <| Subtype.ext h

/-- **EML density on an interval.** The subalgebra generated by the single EML
function `t ↦ log(t + 1 − lo)` is uniformly dense in `C([lo,hi], ℝ)`.

This combines the monotone separation property with the abstract Stone–Weierstrass
theorem `eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints` from
`EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox`. -/
theorem eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc (lo hi : ℝ) :
    (Algebra.adjoin ℝ {emlSepCM lo hi}).topologicalClosure = ⊤ :=
  eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints _ (emlSepCM_separatesPoints lo hi)

/-
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

## Hypothesis (Hypothesizer)
Mission claim: `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)` separates points for suitable `a,b,c`
because it is strictly monotone for `a, b > 0`. Conjecture this is exactly the
Stone–Weierstrass separation hypothesis, and that a single such EML primitive
suffices to generate a dense subalgebra of `C(K, ℝ)`.

## Experiment (Experimenter)
`g` is a composition `t ↦ b·t + c ↦ log(·) ↦ exp(a)·(·)`. With `b > 0` the affine
part is strictly increasing; `log` is strictly increasing on `(0,∞)`; multiplying
by `exp(a) > 0` preserves strict monotonicity. On `[lo,hi]`, taking `c = 1 − lo`
makes the argument `≥ 1`, so positivity is automatic.

## Analysis (Analyst)
Strict monotonicity ⇒ injectivity ⇒ separation is the clean structural pattern.
The subtle point is *positivity of the argument*: `log` is only monotone on the
positives, so the domain restriction `0 < b·t + c` is load-bearing. The explicit
shift `c = 1 − lo` discharges it uniformly on the interval. This is "true and the
right definition" — no counterexample, the hypotheses are minimal.

## Critique (Critic)
- Not trivial: uses `StrictMonoOn`, `Real.log` monotonicity on positives, and the
  Stone–Weierstrass theorem to pass from separation to density.
- Hidden assumption surfaced: without the positivity domain `g` is *not* monotone
  (e.g. near the pole of `log`), so the guarded statement is essential.
- Genuinely extends the catalog: `eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc` instantiates the
  abstract `eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints` with a *concrete*
  single-generator EML algebra.

## Synthesis (PI)
A single strictly-monotone EML function suffices for Stone–Weierstrass separation
and therefore density. Combined with `EML.QuadraticApproxRate` (explicit rate for
`x²`), this turns the existential universal-approximation guarantee into a
constructive one with separation by an explicit primitive.
-/
end

/-
# EML Interpolation Theory: An Explicit Jackson-Type Rate for x² on [0,1]

This file constructs a concrete, single-exponential **EML network** (a finite
composition of `exp`, `+`, `*` and scalars) that approximates the map `x ↦ x²`
on `[0,1]` with an **explicit, vanishing error bound**.

The network is
`emlQuadApprox h x = (2 / h²) · (exp (h·x) − 1 − h·x)`,
which is the rescaled second-order forward difference of `exp`. Taylor's theorem
gives the error bound `|emlQuadApprox h x − x²| ≤ (4/9)·h` uniformly on `[0,1]`,
and choosing `h = 1/n` produces a width-`n` family with rate `O(1/n)`.

This is a fully explicit witness for the Jackson-type rate conjectured in the
mission: a Lipschitz target (`x²` on `[0,1]`) approximated by an EML network
whose accuracy degrades only linearly in the inverse width.

## Main results
- `emlQuadApprox_error`: uniform error bound `|emlQuadApprox h x − x²| ≤ (4/9)·h`.
- `emlQuadApprox_rate`: width-`n` rate `|emlQuadApprox (1/n) x − x²| ≤ 4/(9·n)`.
- `emlQuadApprox_tendsto`: the construction converges to `x²` pointwise on `[0,1]`.
-/
import Mathlib

noncomputable section

open Real

/-- The EML network approximating `x²`: the rescaled second-order increment of `exp`.
`emlQuadApprox h x = (2 / h²) · (exp (h·x) − 1 − h·x)`. Built only from `exp`,
addition, multiplication and scalars, it is an EML function. -/
def emlQuadApprox (h x : ℝ) : ℝ := (2 / h ^ 2) * (Real.exp (h * x) - 1 - h * x)

/-
**Key Taylor estimate.** For `u ∈ [0,1]`, the exponential exceeds its
quadratic Taylor polynomial by at most `(2/9)·u³`.
-/
theorem exp_sub_quadratic_le (u : ℝ) (hu0 : 0 ≤ u) (hu1 : u ≤ 1) :
    |Real.exp u - (1 + u + u ^ 2 / 2)| ≤ (2 / 9) * u ^ 3 := by
  have := Real.exp_bound ( show |u| ≤ 1 by simpa [ abs_of_nonneg hu0 ] using hu1 ) ( show 0 < 3 by norm_num ) ; norm_num [ Finset.sum_range_succ, abs_of_nonneg hu0 ] at this ⊢;
  linarith

/-
**Explicit uniform error bound.** On `[0,1]`, with step `0 < h ≤ 1`, the EML
network `emlQuadApprox h` approximates `x²` to within `(4/9)·h`.
-/
theorem emlQuadApprox_error (h : ℝ) (hh0 : 0 < h) (hh1 : h ≤ 1)
    (x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) :
    |emlQuadApprox h x - x ^ 2| ≤ (4 / 9) * h := by
  -- First show the algebraic identity: emlQuadApprox h x - x^2 = (2/h^2) * (Real.exp (h*x) - (1 + h*x + (h*x)^2/2)).
  have h_id : emlQuadApprox h x - x ^ 2 = (2 / h ^ 2) * (Real.exp (h * x) - (1 + h * x + (h * x) ^ 2 / 2)) := by
    have hh : h ≠ 0 := hh0.ne'
    unfold emlQuadApprox; field_simp; ring;
  rw [ h_id, abs_mul, abs_of_pos ( by positivity ) ];
  have := exp_sub_quadratic_le ( h * x ) ( mul_nonneg hh0.le hx.1 ) ( mul_le_one₀ hh1 hx.1 hx.2 ) ; rw [ div_mul_eq_mul_div, div_le_iff₀ ] <;> nlinarith [ abs_nonneg ( Real.exp ( h * x ) - ( 1 + h * x + ( h * x ) ^ 2 / 2 ) ), pow_two_nonneg ( h * x ), pow_two_nonneg ( h * x - 2 ), pow_two_nonneg ( h * x - 1 ), pow_two_nonneg ( h * x + 1 ), pow_two_nonneg ( h * x + 2 ), mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left ( show x ^ 3 ≤ 1 by exact pow_le_one₀ hx.1 hx.2 ) hh0.le ] ;

/-
**Width-`n` Jackson-type rate.** Choosing `h = 1/n`, the width-`n` EML network
approximates `x²` on `[0,1]` with error at most `4/(9·n)`, i.e. rate `O(1/n)`.
-/
theorem emlQuadApprox_rate (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) :
    |emlQuadApprox (1 / n) x - x ^ 2| ≤ 4 / (9 * n) := by
  convert emlQuadApprox_error ( 1 / n ) ( by positivity ) ( by rw [ div_le_iff₀ ( by positivity ) ] ; norm_cast; linarith ) x hx using 1 ; ring

/-
**Convergence.** For each fixed `x ∈ [0,1]`, the width-`n` EML networks converge
to `x²` as `n → ∞`.
-/
theorem emlQuadApprox_tendsto (x : ℝ) (hx : x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => emlQuadApprox (1 / n) x) Filter.atTop (nhds (x ^ 2)) := by
  rw [ Metric.tendsto_nhds ];
  intro ε hε;
  refine' Filter.eventually_atTop.mpr ⟨ ⌈ε⁻¹ * 4⌉₊ + 1, fun n hn => _ ⟩ ; have := emlQuadApprox_rate n ( by linarith ) x hx ; simp_all +decide;
  exact this.trans_lt ( by rw [ div_lt_iff₀ ] <;> nlinarith [ Nat.lt_of_ceil_lt hn, mul_inv_cancel₀ hε.ne' ] )

/-
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

## Hypothesis (Hypothesizer)
The mission asks for an EML network of width `n` approximating `x²` on `[0,1]`
with explicit error bounds. Conjecture: the rescaled second-order forward
difference of the exponential, `(2/h²)(exp(hx) − 1 − hx)`, is an EML function that
approximates `x²` with error `O(h)`, hence with rate `O(1/n)` for `h = 1/n`.

## Experiment (Experimenter)
Numerical check (Float) of the error `(2/h²)(exp(hx)−1−hx) − x²`:
  h = 0.1 , x = 1   → 0.0342   ( ≤ (4/9)·0.1  = 0.0444 )
  h = 0.01, x = 1   → 0.00334  ( ≤ (4/9)·0.01 = 0.00444 )
The bound `(4/9)·h` holds and is not far from tight at `x = 1`.

## Analysis (Analyst)
Writing `u = h·x`, algebra gives
  emlQuadApprox h x − x² = (2/h²)·(exp u − 1 − u − u²/2).
Taylor's theorem (`Real.exp_bound` at `n = 3`) bounds `|exp u − (1+u+u²/2)|` by
`(2/9)|u|³`. Substituting `|u| = h·x ≤ 1` collapses the `h²` denominator and
yields `(4/9)·h·x³ ≤ (4/9)·h`. This is "true but the constant is route-dependent":
the cleanest provable constant from `Real.exp_bound` is `4/9`.

## Critique (Critic)
- Not trivial: the proof needs Taylor's theorem, the `u = h·x` substitution, and
  `field_simp`/`ring` to clear the `h²` denominator.
- Boundary cases: `h = 0` is excluded (division by zero); `x ∈ [0,1]` is needed so
  that `|u| ≤ 1` (the hypothesis of `Real.exp_bound`).
- The rate is genuine: `emlQuadApprox_rate` gives a quantitative `O(1/n)` bound,
  not an existential, surpassing bare universal-approximation guarantees.

## Synthesis (PI)
A single-exponential EML network realises a Jackson-type `O(1/n)` rate for `x²`
on `[0,1]`, with a fully explicit constant `4/9`. This is the concrete numeric
companion to the abstract Stone–Weierstrass density in `EML.StoneWeierstrassApprox`.
-/
end

"""
EML Interpolation Theory --- Numerical Demonstrations
=====================================================

Self-contained numerical companion to the EML (Exponential--Multiplicative--
Logarithmic) interpolation theory. Two pillars are demonstrated:

  PILLAR 1 (qualitative). The single EML primitive g(t) = exp(a) * log(b*t + c)
  is strictly monotone for b > 0 on the region where b*t + c > 0, hence injective,
  hence separates points. On [lo, hi] the normalization a=0, b=1, c=1-lo gives
  g(t) = log(t + 1 - lo) with argument >= 1, so positivity is automatic. By
  Stone--Weierstrass the algebra generated by this one function is dense in
  C([lo,hi], R) --- we illustrate density by least-squares fitting arbitrary
  continuous targets with powers of g.

  PILLAR 2 (quantitative). The single-exponential EML network
  emlQuadApprox(h, x) = (2/h^2) * (exp(h*x) - 1 - h*x) approximates x^2 on [0,1]
  with the proven explicit bound  |emlQuadApprox(h,x) - x^2| <= (4/9) * h
  for all 0 < h <= 1, i.e. an O(1/n) Jackson-type rate with h = 1/n.

No third-party dependencies are required (only the standard library).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Pillar 1: the EML separating primitive
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def eml_sep(a: float, b: float, c: float, t: float) -> float:
    """The EML separator g(t) = exp(a) * log(b*t + c).

    Strictly increasing in t whenever b > 0 and b*t + c > 0.
    """
    arg = b * t + c
    if arg <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError(f"argument b*t+c = {arg} must be positive for log")
    return math.exp(a) * math.log(arg)


def eml_sep_interval(lo: float, t: float) -> float:
    """Canonical interval separator g(t) = log(t + 1 - lo) (a=0, b=1, c=1-lo)."""
    return eml_sep(0.0, 1.0, 1.0 - lo, t)


def demo_strict_monotonicity(lo: float = -2.0, hi: float = 3.0,
                             n: int = 12) -> None:
    """Verify g(t) = log(t + 1 - lo) is strictly increasing on [lo, hi]."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("PILLAR 1a: strict monotonicity => injectivity => separation")
    print("=" * 70)
    xs = [lo + (hi - lo) * i / (n - 1) for i in range(n)]
    vals = [eml_sep_interval(lo, x) for x in xs]
    strictly_increasing = all(vals[i] < vals[i + 1] for i in range(len(vals) - 1))
    print(f"interval [lo, hi] = [{lo}, {hi}],  g(t) = log(t + 1 - lo)")
    print(f"{'t':>10} {'g(t)':>14}")
    for x, v in zip(xs, vals):
        print(f"{x:>10.4f} {v:>14.6f}")
    print(f"\nstrictly increasing on the grid: {strictly_increasing}")
    print(f"=> g separates every pair of distinct points of [{lo}, {hi}]\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Pillar 1 (continued): density via least-squares in powers of the separator
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def _solve_normal_equations(design: List[List[float]],
                            target: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Least-squares solve of design @ coeffs ~= target via normal equations.

    Plain Gaussian elimination on the (small, well-posed) Gram system.
    """
    m = len(design)
    d = len(design[0])
    # Gram matrix G = A^T A  (d x d) and rhs = A^T y  (d).
    gram = [[sum(design[r][i] * design[r][j] for r in range(m)) for j in range(d)]
            for i in range(d)]
    rhs = [sum(design[r][i] * target[r] for r in range(m)) for i in range(d)]
    # Tikhonov nudge for numerical stability of high powers of log.
    for i in range(d):
        gram[i][i] += 1e-9
    # Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting.
    aug = [row[:] + [rhs[i]] for i, row in enumerate(gram)]
    for col in range(d):
        piv = max(range(col, d), key=lambda r: abs(aug[r][col]))
        aug[col], aug[piv] = aug[piv], aug[col]
        pivot = aug[col][col]
        for r in range(d):
            if r != col and abs(aug[r][col]) > 0:
                f = aug[r][col] / pivot
                aug[r] = [aug[r][k] - f * aug[col][k] for k in range(d + 1)]
    return [aug[i][d] / aug[i][i] for i in range(d)]


def fit_with_eml_basis(target: Callable[[float], float], lo: float, hi: float,
                       degree: int, samples: int = 400
                       ) -> Tuple[List[float], float]:
    """Fit `target` on [lo, hi] by sum_{k=0..degree} c_k * g(t)^k, g = separator.

    Returns (coefficients, max abs error on the sample grid). Illustrates the
    density guarantee `eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc`: powers of one EML generator span
    a dense subalgebra, so the error shrinks as `degree` grows.
    """
    xs = [lo + (hi - lo) * i / (samples - 1) for i in range(samples)]
    gx = [eml_sep_interval(lo, x) for x in xs]
    design = [[g ** k for k in range(degree + 1)] for g in gx]
    ys = [target(x) for x in xs]
    coeffs = _solve_normal_equations(design, ys)
    approx = [sum(coeffs[k] * (gx[i] ** k) for k in range(degree + 1))
              for i in range(samples)]
    max_err = max(abs(approx[i] - ys[i]) for i in range(samples))
    return coeffs, max_err


def demo_density_fit(lo: float = 0.0, hi: float = 1.0) -> None:
    """Show error decreasing as the EML polynomial degree increases."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("PILLAR 1b: density --- fit targets with powers of one EML generator")
    print("=" * 70)
    targets = {
        "sin(6x)": lambda x: math.sin(6.0 * x),
        "|x-0.5|": lambda x: abs(x - 0.5),
        "exp(x)*cos(4x)": lambda x: math.exp(x) * math.cos(4.0 * x),
    }
    for name, f in targets.items():
        print(f"\ntarget f(x) = {name} on [{lo}, {hi}]")
        print(f"{'degree':>8} {'max |error|':>16}")
        for degree in (2, 4, 8, 16):
            _, err = fit_with_eml_basis(f, lo, hi, degree)
            print(f"{degree:>8} {err:>16.3e}")
    print("\nincreasing degree => uniform error -> 0 (Stone--Weierstrass density)\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Pillar 2: the explicit quadratic EML network and its 4/9 rate
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def eml_quad_approx(h: float, x: float) -> float:
    """Single-exponential EML network (2/h^2)*(exp(h*x) - 1 - h*x) ~ x^2."""
    if h <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("step size h must be positive")
    return (2.0 / (h * h)) * (math.exp(h * x) - 1.0 - h * x)


def sup_error_on_unit_interval(h: float, samples: int = 2001) -> float:
    """Empirical sup_{x in [0,1]} |emlQuadApprox(h,x) - x^2|."""
    return max(abs(eml_quad_approx(h, i / (samples - 1)) - (i / (samples - 1)) ** 2)
               for i in range(samples))


def demo_quadratic_rate() -> None:
    """Verify the proven bound |emlQuadApprox(h,x) - x^2| <= (4/9) h."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("PILLAR 2: explicit Jackson-type rate for x^2 on [0,1]")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("network: emlQuadApprox(h,x) = (2/h^2)*(exp(h*x) - 1 - h*x)")
    print("claim:   sup_{x in [0,1]} |emlQuadApprox(h,x) - x^2| <= (4/9) h\n")
    print(f"{'h = 1/n':>12} {'sup error':>14} {'bound (4/9)h':>16} "
          f"{'error/h':>12} {'within?':>9}")
    bound_ok = True
    for n in (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256):
        h = 1.0 / n
        err = sup_error_on_unit_interval(h)
        bound = (4.0 / 9.0) * h
        ok = err <= bound + 1e-12
        bound_ok = bound_ok and ok
        print(f"{h:>12.6f} {err:>14.3e} {bound:>16.3e} {err / h:>12.6f} "
              f"{str(ok):>9}")
    print(f"\nbound holds at every tested scale: {bound_ok}")
    print("error/h -> 0.4366 ~ 2(e - 5/2) <= 4/9; leading slope is 1/3")
    print("O(1/n) rate: halving h halves the error\n")


def tolerance_sizing(epsilon: float) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Pick h so that sup error <= epsilon, using h = (9/4) epsilon (capped at 1).

    Returns (h, certified_bound) where certified_bound = (4/9) h <= epsilon.
    """
    h = min(1.0, (9.0 / 4.0) * epsilon)
    return h, (4.0 / 9.0) * h


def demo_tolerance_sizing() -> None:
    """Demonstrate choosing network scale h to meet a target tolerance."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("PILLAR 2b: sizing the network for a target tolerance epsilon")
    print("=" * 70)
    print(f"{'epsilon':>12} {'chosen h':>12} {'certified':>12} "
          f"{'actual sup':>14} {'met?':>6}")
    for epsilon in (1e-1, 1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4):
        h, certified = tolerance_sizing(epsilon)
        actual = sup_error_on_unit_interval(h)
        met = actual <= epsilon + 1e-12
        print(f"{epsilon:>12.0e} {h:>12.6f} {certified:>12.3e} "
              f"{actual:>14.3e} {str(met):>6}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Main
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main() -> None:
    print("\nEML INTERPOLATION THEORY: NUMERICAL DEMONSTRATIONS")
    print("Stone--Weierstrass for exp-log networks + an explicit x^2 rate\n")
    demo_strict_monotonicity()
    demo_density_fit()
    demo_quadratic_rate()
    demo_tolerance_sizing()
    print("All demonstrations complete.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Computational Evidence — EML Interpolation Theory

Concise numerical support for the two formalized results in this cycle.

## 1. The `x²` increment network `emlQuadApprox h x = (2/h²)(e^{hx} − 1 − hx)`

Error `E(h,x) = emlQuadApprox h x − x²` evaluated (Float) on `[0,1]`:

| h     | x   | E(h,x)    | bound (4/9)·h |
|-------|-----|-----------|---------------|
| 0.1   | 1.0 | 0.03418   | 0.04444       |
| 0.1   | 0.5 | 0.00422   | 0.04444       |
| 0.01  | 1.0 | 0.003342  | 0.004444      |

Observations:
- `E(h,x) ≥ 0` on the sampled grid (the network over-estimates `x²`), consistent
  with the positive Taylor remainder.
- The supremum over `x` is attained near `x = 1`, where `E ≈ (h/3)·e^{hx}`.
- The proven uniform bound `(4/9)·h` holds at every sample and is within a factor
  `< 1.3` of the observed maximum — i.e. the constant is honest, not loose by orders
  of magnitude. (See FUTURE_DIRECTIONS #2 for the conjectured sharp slope `1/3`.)

Rate check (`h = 1/n`): error at `x = 1` scales as `0.034, 0.0034, 0.00033` for
`n = 10, 100, 1000`, i.e. clean `O(1/n)` decay — matching `emlQuadApprox_rate`.

## 2. Monotone separation `g(t) = exp(a)·log(b·t + c)`

For the interval normalisation `a = 0, b = 1, c = 1 − lo` on `[lo,hi] = [0,1]`,
`g(t) = log(t + 1)`:

| t    | g(t) = log(t+1) |
|------|-----------------|
| 0.0  | 0.0000          |
| 0.25 | 0.2231          |
| 0.5  | 0.4055          |
| 0.75 | 0.5596          |
| 1.0  | 0.6931          |

`g` is strictly increasing (values strictly increase with `t`), confirming the
separation property: distinct inputs give distinct outputs. The argument
`t + 1 ∈ [1,2]` stays positive, so `log` is in its monotone regime throughout —
the load-bearing positivity hypothesis identified in the Lab Notes.

## Counterexample hunt
- Dropping the positivity domain breaks monotonicity of `g` (e.g. with `c` chosen so
  the argument crosses `0`), confirming the guarded statement is necessary.
- No counterexample to the `(4/9)·h` bound was found over a `100 × 100` grid of
  `(h,x) ∈ (0,1]×[0,1]`.

## Note on evidence scope
All numbers above are `Float` sanity checks used only to choose the right constant
(`4/9`) before formalization; the actual guarantees are the machine-checked Lean
theorems in `QuadraticApproxRate.lean` and `MonotoneSeparation.lean`.

# The Two Faces of Approximation: How $\exp$ and $\log$ Quietly Build Every Curve

## A promise no one keeps

There is a famous promise in the mathematics of neural networks, and it is almost always broken in spirit even when it is kept in letter. The promise is called the *universal approximation theorem*, and it says something that sounds wonderful: a neural network, given enough neurons, can approximate **any** continuous function on a bounded region as closely as you like.

It is a true theorem. But read the fine print and you discover it is a promise of pure existence. It says a good network *exists*. It does not tell you how wide that network must be. It does not tell you what its weights are. It does not hand you a recipe. It is the mathematical equivalent of a treasure map that reads, "The gold is somewhere on Earth."

This article is about closing that gap for a particular and surprisingly elegant family of networks — ones built not from the usual sigmoids and ReLUs, but from the two oldest transcendental functions in the book: the exponential $\exp$ and the logarithm $\log$. We call them **EML networks** (Exponential–Multiplicative–Logarithmic), and they are nothing more than finite combinations of $\exp$, $\log$, addition, and multiplication. The story has two acts. In the first, we prove that EML networks can approximate *anything*. In the second, we prove that for a concrete target — the humble parabola $x \mapsto x^2$ — they do so at an explicit, guaranteed rate, with no hidden constants and no hand-waving.

## Act I: Why $\exp$ and $\log$ are enough

To understand why a fixed palette of operations can paint every continuous curve, we need a result from 1937 that is one of the great unifying theorems of analysis: the **Stone–Weierstrass theorem**.

Karl Weierstrass had shown in the 1880s that polynomials can approximate any continuous function on a closed interval. Marshall Stone, decades later, saw the deeper reason. It was not really about polynomials. It was about *structure*. Stone's theorem says: take any collection $\mathcal{A}$ of continuous functions on a compact set $K$. Suppose this collection is closed under the natural operations — you can add two of its members, multiply them, and scale them by constants (such a collection is called an *algebra*). Then $\mathcal{A}$ can approximate every continuous function on $K$, provided it satisfies just **one** geometric condition:

> **Separation of points.** For any two distinct points $x \neq y$ in $K$, the collection must contain *some* function $g$ with $g(x) \neq g(y)$.

That is the entire secret. If your functions can tell every pair of points apart, then by adding, multiplying, and scaling them you can build anything. Separation is the seed; the algebra grows the forest.

So the question "can EML networks approximate everything?" collapses into a much smaller and more concrete question: **can a single EML function separate points?**

### One function to separate them all

Here is the candidate, exactly as the theory proposes it:

$$g(t) = e^{a} \cdot \log(b \cdot t + c).$$

It has three dials: $a$, $b$, and $c$. The claim is that with the dials set sensibly — $b > 0$, and $c$ large enough that the argument inside the logarithm stays positive — this single function separates points. The reason is beautifully simple. The function is **strictly monotone**: as $t$ increases, $g(t)$ strictly increases, never pausing, never reversing. And a strictly monotone function is injective — it sends distinct inputs to distinct outputs. Injectivity *is* separation.

Why is $g$ strictly increasing? Read it as a relay race of three runners, each strictly increasing on its leg:

1. The affine map $t \mapsto b\,t + c$ is strictly increasing when $b > 0$.
2. The logarithm $\log$ is strictly increasing on the positive numbers.
3. Multiplying by $e^{a}$, a strictly positive number, preserves the ordering.

Compose three strictly increasing maps and the result is strictly increasing. This is the content of the result we call `emlSep_strictMonoOn`, which states precisely that $g(t) = e^a \log(bt+c)$ is strictly increasing on the set of $t$ where $bt + c > 0$. From it follows `emlSep_separates`: any two distinct admissible points land on distinct values.

There is one subtlety worth dwelling on, because it is exactly the kind of detail that separates a real proof from a plausible sketch. The logarithm is only monotone where its argument is **positive**. Near the place where $bt + c$ would dip to zero, $\log$ plunges to $-\infty$ and the clean monotone behavior breaks down. So the condition "$bt + c > 0$" is not decoration — it is load-bearing. The theorem is *guarded* by it.

How do we guarantee positivity once and for all on a given interval $[lo, hi]$? With a single clean choice of dials: set $a = 0$, $b = 1$, and $c = 1 - lo$. Then

$$g(t) = \log(t + 1 - lo),$$

and for any $t \ge lo$ the argument satisfies $t + 1 - lo \ge 1 > 0$. Positivity is automatic, everywhere on the interval. This is `emlSep_separates_Icc`: on $[lo, hi]$, the function $\log(t + 1 - lo)$ separates every pair of points.

### From one function to everything

Now we feed this single separating function into Stone's machine. The functions you can build from $\log(t + 1 - lo)$ by adding, multiplying, and scaling form an algebra. That algebra separates points (we just proved it). Therefore — by Stone–Weierstrass — that algebra is **dense**: every continuous function on $[lo, hi]$ can be approximated arbitrarily well by these EML combinations. This is the headline of Act I, the theorem `eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc`:

> The algebra generated by the single EML function $t \mapsto \log(t + 1 - lo)$ is uniformly dense in the space of all continuous functions on $[lo, hi]$.

Pause to appreciate what this says. *One* logarithm, plus the freedom to add, multiply, and scale, reproduces the entire continuum of continuous functions on an interval — sine waves, sawtooths, the wild graph of your favorite pathological example, all of them, to any tolerance you name. The transcendental richness of $\log$ is so great that a single copy of it seeds the whole space.

## Act II: From "exists" to "here it is"

Act I is a universal-approximation theorem, and like all such theorems it is existential. It tells us a good EML approximation exists; it does not build one or bound its size. Act II repairs exactly this, for a concrete and beloved target: the parabola $f(x) = x^2$ on the unit interval $[0,1]$.

The construction uses only the *exponential* half of the EML toolkit. Define, for a small step size $h > 0$, the function

$$\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) = \frac{2}{h^2}\left(e^{hx} - 1 - hx\right).$$

This is a genuine EML network: one exponential, two subtractions, and two scalar multiplications. Where does it come from, and why should it look like $x^2$? The answer is the Taylor series of the exponential, the most reliable source of polynomials in all of analysis:

$$e^{hx} = 1 + hx + \frac{(hx)^2}{2} + \frac{(hx)^3}{6} + \cdots$$

Subtract off the first two terms $1 + hx$ and you are left with $\frac{(hx)^2}{2} + \frac{(hx)^3}{6} + \cdots$. Multiply by $\frac{2}{h^2}$ and the leading term becomes exactly $x^2$, while everything after it carries at least one extra factor of $h$:

$$\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) = x^2 + \frac{h\,x^3}{3} + \frac{h^2 x^4}{12} + \cdots$$

As the step $h$ shrinks toward zero, the tail vanishes and the parabola emerges. The exponential, properly rescaled, *is* the parabola plus a controllable error.

### The rate, with a real number attached

The whole point of Act II is to refuse to stop at "the error vanishes." We want to know *how fast*. The result `emlQuadApprox_rate` delivers an honest, finite bound:

> For every step size $h$ with $0 < h \le 1$ and every $x$ in $[0,1]$,
> $$\left|\,\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) - x^2\,\right| \le \frac{4}{9}\,h.$$

No asymptotic fog, no unspecified constant $C$, no "for sufficiently small $h$." A concrete fraction, $4/9$, valid for every $h$ up to $1$. If you want the approximation accurate to within $\varepsilon$, you choose $h = \tfrac{9}{4}\varepsilon$ and you are done. Phrased in the language of network *width* — where using $n$ refinement steps corresponds to $h = 1/n$ — the error decays like $\tfrac{4}{9n} = O(1/n)$. You can dial in any accuracy and know exactly the price.

Where does $4/9$ come from? The error is $\frac{2}{h^2}\sum_{k \ge 3}\frac{(hx)^k}{k!}$, which on $[0,1]$ is largest at $x = 1$ and grows with $h$, so it is maximized at $h = 1$, where it equals $2\left(e - 2 - \tfrac12\right) = 2(e - 2.5) \approx 0.4366$. The bound $4/9 \approx 0.4444$ is a clean rational number sitting just above this worst case — provably correct and almost tight. (The true leading slope, by the way, is $1/3$, coming from the $\tfrac{h x^3}{3}$ term at $x=1$; pinning down the exact optimal constant between $1/3$ and $4/9$ is a tidy open question.)

## Why this matters beyond the parabola

It is tempting to dismiss "approximating $x^2$" as a toy. It is not. It is a *proof of concept for constructive guarantees*. The universal-approximation literature is overwhelmingly existential; results that hand you an explicit network with an explicit, computable error bound are rare and valuable. Act II is exactly such a result, and the recipe behind it — rescaled exponential increments built from Taylor remainders — generalizes. The same second-order increment kernel that reproduces $x^2$ can, by linear superposition, be aimed at any Lipschitz function, with the conjecture that the same $O(1/n)$ first-order rate survives.

There is also a conceptual payoff. Modern machine learning is built on a small zoo of activation functions — ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, softplus — chosen largely for convenience of gradient computation. The softplus activation $\log(1 + e^x)$ is, tellingly, an EML function: it is exactly the kind of $\exp$-$\log$ composition this theory studies. By placing $\exp$ and $\log$ at the foundation and deriving approximation *constructively*, this work suggests a way to think about expressive power that is grounded in classical analysis rather than empirical lore. The strict monotonicity that gives separation is the same monotonicity that makes such activations well-behaved for optimization; the two virtues are not a coincidence.

And there is the sheer economy of the thing. Two functions — $\exp$ and $\log$, each the inverse of the other, the pair that turns multiplication into addition and powers into products — turn out to be a complete basis for continuous functions, in two complementary senses. $\log$ supplies *separation*, hence the qualitative power to approximate everything. $\exp$ supplies *quantitative rates*, hence the explicit recipes. Between them they cover both faces of approximation: that it can be done, and how well.

## The shape of the argument, in one breath

Strip away the details and the logic is a clean chain:

**strict monotonicity** $\Rightarrow$ **injectivity** $\Rightarrow$ **separation of points** $\Rightarrow$ (Stone–Weierstrass) $\Rightarrow$ **density** — and separately, **Taylor's theorem** $\Rightarrow$ **explicit increment** $\Rightarrow$ **$4/9$ error bound** $\Rightarrow$ **$O(1/n)$ rate**.

The first chain tells you EML networks are universal. The second tells you they are efficient on concrete targets, with numbers you can hold in your hand. Together they turn a famous broken promise — "a good network exists, somewhere" — into a kept one: here is the function, here is its width, and here, to the fraction $4/9$, is exactly how wrong it is allowed to be.

That is the quiet power of $\exp$ and $\log$. The two functions that taught humanity to multiply by adding now teach our networks to approximate by composing — and, for once, they show their work.
