# EML Interpolation Theory: A Stone–Weierstrass Framework for Exponential–Logarithmic Networks with Explicit Jackson-Type Rates

**Author:** Aristotle

**Date:** 2026-06-27

**Domain:** Novelty (Approximation Theory / Foundations of Neural Networks)

---

## Abstract

We develop a constructive approximation theory for **EML networks** — function classes generated from the transcendental primitives $\exp$ and $\log$ together with addition, multiplication, and scalar multiplication. The theory has two complementary pillars. First, a **qualitative** pillar: we identify a single explicit EML primitive, $g(t) = e^{a}\log(bt+c)$, prove it is strictly monotone (hence injective, hence point-separating) on the region where its argument is positive, and feed it into the Stone–Weierstrass theorem to conclude that the subalgebra it generates is uniformly dense in $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$. The normalization $a=0$, $b=1$, $c=1-lo$ discharges the positivity side-condition uniformly on any interval, yielding a one-generator dense EML algebra. Second, a **quantitative** pillar: we exhibit a concrete single-exponential EML network $\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) = \tfrac{2}{h^2}(e^{hx}-1-hx)$ and prove the explicit, non-asymptotic uniform bound $\|\text{emlQuadApprox}_h - (\cdot)^2\|_{\infty,[0,1]} \le \tfrac{4}{9}h$ for all $0 < h \le 1$, giving an $O(1/n)$ Jackson-type rate (with $h=1/n$) for approximating $x^2$ on $[0,1]$. The two pillars convert the existential universal-approximation guarantee into a constructive one, with separation realized by an explicit primitive and rates carrying explicit constants. All results discussed here are fully formalized and machine-checked; this paper presents the mathematics, statements, and proof sketches.

**Keywords:** EML networks, exp-log functions, Stone–Weierstrass theorem, separation of points, strict monotonicity, universal approximation, Jackson-type rate, softplus, constructive approximation.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 The existential gap

The universal approximation theorem (UAT) for neural networks asserts that a sufficiently wide single-hidden-layer network with a non-polynomial activation is dense in $C(K)$ for compact $K$. As classically stated it is an *existence* result: it guarantees an approximant without specifying width, weights, or an error constant. For applications — and for a foundational understanding of *why* a given activation class is expressive — one wants more: an explicit separating primitive (to certify density from first principles) and explicit, computable approximation rates (to size networks for a target tolerance).

### 1.2 EML networks

We study the function class generated by the two canonical transcendental functions and the field operations.

> **Definition 1 (EML function class, informal).** An *EML function* on a domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is any function obtained by finitely many compositions of the primitives $\exp$, $\log$ (on positive arguments), addition $+$, multiplication $\times$, and multiplication by real scalars, starting from coordinate projections and constants.

This class is natural for several reasons. It is closed under the operations defining a subalgebra of $C(K,\mathbb{R})$, making Stone–Weierstrass directly applicable. It contains the **softplus** activation $\log(1+e^x)$ and its relatives, which appear throughout machine learning. And $\exp$ and $\log$ are mutually inverse strictly monotone bijections of $\mathbb{R}$ and $(0,\infty)$, a structural fact we exploit twice: $\log$ for separation, $\exp$ for rates.

### 1.3 Historical context

Three classical landmarks frame this work. **Weierstrass (1885)** proved that polynomials are uniformly dense in $C([a,b],\mathbb{R})$. **Stone (1937, 1948)** abstracted the mechanism: density follows from algebraic closure plus point separation, on any compact Hausdorff space. **Jackson (1911)** quantified the polynomial case, bounding the best uniform approximation error of a function by its smoothness (e.g. $O(1/n)$ for Lipschitz functions by degree-$n$ polynomials). The modern *universal approximation theorems* for neural networks (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991; Leshno et al. 1993; Pinkus 1999) are descendants of the Stone–Weierstrass circle of ideas, but most are stated existentially. Our aim is to give the EML class both a Stone-style qualitative theory (with an *explicit* separator) and a Jackson-style quantitative theory (with an *explicit* constant), for a transcendental primitive set rather than for polynomials.

### 1.4 Why $\exp$ and $\log$, specifically

The pair $(\exp,\log)$ is distinguished among transcendental functions. They are mutually inverse, each a strictly monotone bijection ($\exp:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty)$, $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$), and together they intertwine the additive and multiplicative structures of $\mathbb{R}$ via $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$ and $e^{x+y}=e^xe^y$. The monotonicity supplies *separation* with no auxiliary construction, while the analyticity of $\exp$ — its everywhere-convergent Taylor series — supplies *rates* by truncation. Thus the same two primitives cover both halves of approximation theory. They are also of direct practical interest: the softplus activation $\operatorname{softplus}(x)=\log(1+e^x)$, a smooth surrogate for ReLU, is literally an EML function, as are log-sum-exp pooling and many normalizing-flow building blocks.

### 1.5 Contributions

1. **A concrete separating primitive (§3).** We prove $g(t)=e^a\log(bt+c)$ is strictly monotone on $\{t : bt+c>0\}$ for $b>0$ (`emlSep_strictMonoOn`), hence separates points (`emlSep_separates`), with an explicit interval normalization (`emlSep_separates_Icc`).
2. **One-generator EML density (§4).** The subalgebra generated by the single function $t\mapsto \log(t+1-lo)$ separates points of $[lo,hi]$ (`emlSepCM_separatesPoints`) and is therefore uniformly dense in $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$ (`eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc`).
3. **An abstract Stone–Weierstrass / pullback engine (§2, §5).** A reusable framework deriving density of point-separating EML subalgebras, with a density-transfer mechanism along continuous and injective maps (`eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints`, `eml_universalApproximation`, `pullback_dense_of_injective`, `eml_pullback_universalApproximation`).
4. **An explicit Jackson-type rate (§6).** The single-exponential network $\text{emlQuadApprox}_h$ approximates $x^2$ on $[0,1]$ with the explicit bound $\tfrac{4}{9}h$ (`emlQuadApprox_rate`), giving an $O(1/n)$ rate.

---

## 2. Background: the Stone–Weierstrass engine

We work in $C(X,\mathbb{R})$, the continuous real functions on a compact Hausdorff space $X$, with the uniform (supremum) norm $\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x\in X}|f(x)|$. By compactness this supremum is attained, and $(C(X,\mathbb{R}),\|\cdot\|_\infty)$ is a Banach space; uniform convergence is exactly convergence in this norm. A **subalgebra** $A \le C(X,\mathbb{R})$ is a linear subspace closed under pointwise multiplication and containing the constants. The *topological closure* $\overline A$ (also written $A.\text{topologicalClosure}$) is the smallest closed subalgebra containing $A$; saying $\overline A=\top$ is the same as saying $A$ is dense, i.e. every continuous function is a uniform limit of members of $A$.

The organizing principle of the entire development is a single reduction: *density questions for EML algebras reduce to a separation question for a single EML function.* Everything qualitative below is an instance of this reduction; the only creative content is exhibiting the separator (§3) and verifying its side-condition (positivity of the logarithm's argument).

> **Definition 2 (Separation of points).** A set $A \subseteq C(X,\mathbb{R})$ *separates points* if for all $x \neq y$ in $X$ there exists $h \in A$ with $h(x) \neq h(y)$.

> **Theorem 3 (Stone–Weierstrass; `eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints`).** If $A \le C(X,\mathbb{R})$ is a subalgebra that separates points, then its topological closure is all of $C(X,\mathbb{R})$: $\overline{A} = \top$. Equivalently (`eml_dense_range_of_subalgebra_separatesPoints`), $A$ is dense; equivalently (`eml_exists_uniform_approx`), for every $f \in C(X,\mathbb{R})$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $g \in A$ with $\|g-f\|_\infty < \varepsilon$.

*Proof sketch.* This is the classical real Stone–Weierstrass theorem. The closure $\overline{A}$ is a closed subalgebra; one shows it is a sublattice (closed under $\max,\min$) by approximating $|{\cdot}|$ uniformly on a bounded interval by polynomials, hence $|f| = \sqrt{f^2}\in\overline A$, hence $\max(f,g)=\tfrac12(f+g+|f-g|)\in\overline A$. A closed point-separating sublattice containing constants is all of $C(X,\mathbb{R})$ by a two-point interpolation plus compactness argument. $\square$

This reduces *every* density question for EML algebras to the single combinatorial-geometric task of exhibiting separation.

### 2.1 Density transfer along maps (pullback engine)

For multivariate and structured domains it is useful to transport density along a continuous map. Given $\varphi \in C(X,Y)$, precomposition $g \mapsto g\circ\varphi$ is an algebra homomorphism $\text{precompAlgHom}(\varphi): C(Y,\mathbb{R}) \to C(X,\mathbb{R})$.

> **Definition 4 (Pullback subalgebra).** For $A \le C(Y,\mathbb{R})$, define $\varphi^*A := A.\!\operatorname{map}(\text{precompAlgHom}(\varphi)) = \{g\circ\varphi : g\in A\} \le C(X,\mathbb{R})$.

> **Theorem 5 (Injective pullback density; `pullback_dense_of_injective`).** If $X,Y$ are compact Hausdorff, $\varphi:X\to Y$ is continuous and injective, and $A\le C(Y,\mathbb{R})$ is dense ($\overline A=\top$), then $\varphi^*A$ is dense in $C(X,\mathbb{R})$.

*Proof sketch.* Precomposition is norm-contractive, $\|g\circ\varphi - h\circ\varphi\|_\infty \le \|g-h\|_\infty$ (`norm_comp_le`), hence continuous (`continuous_precomp`); so it carries closures into closures and $\overline{\varphi^*A} = \overline{\{g\circ\varphi: g\in\overline A\}}$. The closure of $\varphi^*A$ equals the subalgebra of functions *factoring through* $\varphi$ (`pullback_closure_eq_factorsThrough`), proved by exhibiting that subalgebra as closed: a uniform limit $f$ of functions constant on $\varphi$-fibers is itself constant on fibers, defines a function $\bar g$ on $\operatorname{range}\varphi$, and the Tietze extension theorem extends $\bar g$ to $Y$. When $\varphi$ is injective it is a closed embedding (compact-to-Hausdorff), so *every* $f\in C(X,\mathbb{R})$ factors through it (`factorsThrough_eq_top_of_injective`), again by Tietze. Hence the factors-through subalgebra is $\top$ and $\overline{\varphi^*A}=\top$. $\square$

> **Corollary 6 (`eml_pullback_universalApproximation`, `eml_pullback_exists_approx`).** If $A\le C(Y,\mathbb{R})$ separates points and $\varphi:X\to Y$ is injective continuous, then $\{g\circ\varphi : g\in A\}$ is dense in $C(X,\mathbb{R})$; every $f\in C(X,\mathbb{R})$ is within any $\varepsilon>0$ of some $g\circ\varphi$.

---

## 3. The monotone separation property

We now produce the separating primitive.

> **Definition 7 (EML separator; `emlSep`).** For real parameters $a,b,c$ define
> $$\text{emlSep}(a,b,c)(t) := e^{a}\cdot \log(b\,t + c).$$

> **Theorem 8 (Strict monotonicity; `emlSep_strictMonoOn`).** If $b>0$, then $t \mapsto \text{emlSep}(a,b,c)(t)$ is strictly increasing on the set $\{t \in \mathbb{R} : b\,t+c > 0\}$.

*Proof sketch.* Take $x<y$ with $bx+c>0$ and $by+c>0$. Since $b>0$, $0 < bx+c < by+c$. The logarithm is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$, so $\log(bx+c) < \log(by+c)$. Multiplying by $e^a>0$ preserves the strict inequality: $e^a\log(bx+c) < e^a\log(by+c)$. $\square$

> **Theorem 9 (Separation; `emlSep_separates`).** If $b>0$ and $x\ne y$ with $bx+c>0$, $by+c>0$, then $\text{emlSep}(a,b,c)(x) \ne \text{emlSep}(a,b,c)(y)$.

*Proof sketch.* Strict monotonicity on the positivity region implies injectivity there; distinct admissible inputs give distinct outputs. $\square$

**The positivity guard is essential.** The logarithm is monotone only on $(0,\infty)$; near a zero of $bt+c$ it diverges to $-\infty$ and monotonicity fails. Thus the domain restriction $\{bt+c>0\}$ is not cosmetic but load-bearing. The next result discharges it uniformly on a compact interval.

> **Theorem 10 (Interval separation; `emlSep_separates_Icc`).** For any $lo\le hi$ and distinct $x,y\in[lo,hi]$,
> $$\text{emlSep}(0,1,\,1-lo)(x) \ne \text{emlSep}(0,1,\,1-lo)(y).$$
> Explicitly, the separating function is $g(t)=\log(t+1-lo)$.

*Proof sketch.* With $a=0,b=1,c=1-lo$ the argument is $t+1-lo \ge lo + 1 - lo = 1 > 0$ for all $t\in[lo,hi]$, so positivity holds at both $x$ and $y$; apply Theorem 9 with $b=1>0$. $\square$

---

## 4. One-generator EML density on an interval

We package the separator as an element of $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$ and generate an algebra from it.

> **Definition 11 (Continuous separator; `emlSepCM`).** Let $K=[lo,hi]$ (compact, Hausdorff). Define $\text{emlSepCM}(lo,hi)\in C(K,\mathbb{R})$ by
> $$t \mapsto \log(t + 1 - lo).$$
> Continuity holds because $t+1-lo \ge 1 > 0$ on $K$, so the composition $\log\circ(\text{affine})$ is continuous.

> **Theorem 12 (Generated algebra separates; `emlSepCM_separatesPoints`).** The subalgebra $\operatorname{adjoin}_\mathbb{R}\{\text{emlSepCM}(lo,hi)\}$ separates the points of $[lo,hi]$.

*Proof sketch.* The single generator already separates: for $x\ne y$ in $K$, the generator takes distinct values by Theorem 10. Since the generator lies in the adjoined subalgebra, the subalgebra inherits the separating witness. $\square$

> **Theorem 13 (One-generator density; `eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc`).** The subalgebra generated by the single EML function $t\mapsto\log(t+1-lo)$ is uniformly dense in $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$:
> $$\big(\operatorname{adjoin}_\mathbb{R}\{\text{emlSepCM}(lo,hi)\}\big).\text{topologicalClosure} = \top.$$

*Proof sketch.* Combine Theorem 12 (separation) with Theorem 3 (Stone–Weierstrass): a point-separating subalgebra of $C(K,\mathbb{R})$ over a compact Hausdorff $K$ has closure $\top$. $\square$

**Remark.** Theorem 13 is striking for its economy: a *single* logarithm, plus closure under $+,\times$ and scaling, reproduces all of $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$. The richness of $\log$ as a transcendental seed is what makes one generator suffice.

---

## 5. The abstract EML universal approximation theorem

The interval result is an instance of a general principle, isolated for reuse.

> **Theorem 14 (EML universal approximation; `eml_universalApproximation`).** Let $X$ be compact Hausdorff and let $A \le C(X,\mathbb{R})$ be any subalgebra generated by EML primitives. If $A$ separates points, then $A$ is uniformly dense in $C(X,\mathbb{R})$.

*Proof sketch.* Immediate from Theorem 3; "EML-generated" only matters insofar as it provides a separating member, which is the sole hypothesis used. $\square$

Combined with the pullback engine (§2.1), Theorem 14 extends to structured domains: if a point-separating EML subalgebra lives on $Y$ and $\varphi:X\to Y$ is an injective continuous "feature map," then $\{g\circ\varphi\}$ is dense on $X$ (Corollary 6). This is the route to multivariate EML density: coordinatewise EML separators $g_i(x)=\log(x_i+1-lo_i)$ assembled into a feature map separate points of a box $\prod_i[lo_i,hi_i]$, yielding density on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$ for compact boxes $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ (see §8, Future Directions).

---

## 6. An explicit Jackson-type rate for $x^2$

Density is existential. We now give a *constructive* approximant for a concrete target with an explicit error constant, using only the exponential primitive.

> **Definition 15 (Quadratic EML network; `emlQuadApprox`).** For a step size $h>0$,
> $$\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) := \frac{2}{h^2}\big(e^{hx} - 1 - hx\big).$$
> This is an EML network: one exponential, two subtractions, two scalar multiplications.

> **Lemma 16 (Taylor identity).** For all $h>0$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
> $$\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) = x^2 + \frac{2}{h^2}\sum_{k\ge 3}\frac{(hx)^k}{k!} = x^2 + \frac{h x^3}{3} + \frac{h^2 x^4}{12} + \cdots$$

*Proof sketch.* Expand $e^{hx}=\sum_{k\ge0}(hx)^k/k!$, subtract $1+hx$, leaving $\sum_{k\ge2}(hx)^k/k!$; multiply by $2/h^2$. The $k=2$ term is $\tfrac{2}{h^2}\cdot\tfrac{(hx)^2}{2}=x^2$; the $k\ge3$ terms each carry a positive power of $h$. $\square$

> **Theorem 17 (Explicit rate; `emlQuadApprox_rate`).** For every $h$ with $0<h\le 1$ and every $x\in[0,1]$,
> $$\big|\,\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) - x^2\,\big| \le \frac{4}{9}\,h.$$

*Proof sketch.* By Lemma 16 the error is $E_h(x)=\tfrac{2}{h^2}\sum_{k\ge3}(hx)^k/k! = 2\sum_{k\ge3} h^{k-2}x^k/k! \ge 0$. For $x\in[0,1]$ and $0<h\le1$ each term is increasing in both $x$ and $h$, so the supremum over the square is attained at $x=1,h=1$:
$$\sup E_h(x) \le E_1(1) = 2\sum_{k\ge3}\frac{1}{k!} = 2\Big(e - 1 - 1 - \tfrac12\Big) = 2\big(e-\tfrac52\big) \approx 0.4366.$$
Moreover $E_h(x)\le E_h(1) = 2\sum_{k\ge3}h^{k-2}/k! \le h\cdot 2\sum_{k\ge3}h^{k-3}/k!$, and bounding the remaining series for $0<h\le1$ gives the clean rational majorant $E_h(x)\le \tfrac{4}{9}h$, since $2(e-\tfrac52)\le \tfrac49$. The verification reduces to a finite exponential inequality discharged with standard `Real.exp` bounds. $\square$

> **Corollary 18 ($O(1/n)$ width rate).** Setting $h=1/n$ for a positive integer $n$ yields a single-exponential EML network with
> $$\big\|\,\text{emlQuadApprox}_{1/n} - (\cdot)^2\,\big\|_{\infty,[0,1]} \le \frac{4}{9n} = O\!\left(\frac1n\right).$$
> To achieve uniform error $\le\varepsilon$ it suffices to take $h = \tfrac{9}{4}\varepsilon$ (equivalently $n \ge \tfrac{4}{9\varepsilon}$).

**On tightness.** The empirical worst case $2(e-\tfrac52)\approx 0.4366$ shows the bound $4/9\approx0.4444$ is correct and nearly tight; the leading-order error slope is $1/3$ (the $\tfrac{hx^3}{3}$ term at $x=1$). The exact optimal constant lies in $[\tfrac13,\tfrac49]$; pinning it is a self-contained open problem (§8).

---

## 6b. A worked numerical example

To make the rate concrete, fix $h=\tfrac14$ (i.e. $n=4$). Then for $x\in[0,1]$,
$$\text{emlQuadApprox}_{1/4}(x) = 32\big(e^{x/4} - 1 - \tfrac{x}{4}\big).$$
Theorem 17 guarantees $\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|\text{emlQuadApprox}_{1/4}(x)-x^2|\le \tfrac49\cdot\tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{9}\approx 0.1111$. The true worst-case error, attained near $x=1$, is $\approx 0.0888$, comfortably inside the certificate. Halving the step to $h=\tfrac18$ ($n=8$) provably halves the certificate to $\tfrac{1}{18}\approx0.0556$ and the empirical worst case drops to $\approx0.0430$ — the signature of a first-order $O(1/n)$ method. The following short table (computed by direct evaluation of the closed form) illustrates the geometric decay:

| $n=1/h$ | certificate $\tfrac49 h$ | empirical $\sup$ error | ratio error$/h$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.4444 | 0.4366 | 0.4366 |
| 2 | 0.2222 | 0.1898 | 0.3795 |
| 4 | 0.1111 | 0.0888 | 0.3553 |
| 8 | 0.0556 | 0.0430 | 0.3440 |
| 16 | 0.0278 | 0.0212 | 0.3386 |
| 64 | 0.0069 | 0.0052 | 0.3346 |

The ratio error$/h$ decreases monotonically toward $1/3$, the leading Taylor slope, confirming both that the bound $4/9$ is a valid uniform majorant and that the asymptotically optimal constant is $1/3$ (see §8, Future Direction 2).

## 7. Algorithms

### 7.1 Interval separator / one-generator basis

Given $[lo,hi]$, the canonical separating primitive is $g(t)=\log(t+1-lo)$. Powers and linear combinations $\sum_k c_k\, g(t)^k$ form a dense basis; fitting a target $f$ reduces to least-squares on the design matrix $[\,g(t_i)^k\,]$. Complexity to assemble and solve for degree $d$ at $m$ sample points: $O(md)$ to build, $O(md^2 + d^3)$ to solve.

### 7.2 Quadratic EML network and tolerance sizing

To approximate $x^2$ on $[0,1]$ within $\varepsilon$: choose $h=\tfrac94\varepsilon$ (capped at $1$), return $x\mapsto \tfrac{2}{h^2}(e^{hx}-1-hx)$. Evaluation is $O(1)$ per point (one $\exp$). The guarantee $|{\cdot}|\le\tfrac49 h\le\varepsilon$ is certified, not heuristic.

---

## 8. Applications and discussion

**Constructive UAT.** Theorems 13–14 are density (existential) results, but §3 gives them a *named, explicit* separating witness, and §6 supplies a *fully constructive* approximant with a computable error constant for a concrete target. Together they exemplify the program of upgrading existential universal approximation to constructive approximation with rates.

**Softplus and the ML connection.** The softplus activation $\log(1+e^x)$ is an EML function; the strict monotonicity that yields separation (Theorem 8) is the same property that makes such activations well-conditioned for gradient-based training. EML theory thus offers a classical-analysis foundation for a class of activations used empirically.

**Reusable engine.** The pullback framework (§2.1, §5) is domain-agnostic: any injective continuous feature map transports EML density to a new domain, the mechanism behind multivariate extensions. Concretely, to obtain density on a box $K=\prod_i[lo_i,hi_i]\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ one builds the feature map $\varphi(x)=(g_1(x_1),\dots,g_n(x_n))$ with $g_i(t)=\log(t+1-lo_i)$; each coordinate $g_i$ is injective by Theorem 8, so $\varphi$ is injective, and Corollary 6 transports density of the polynomial algebra on $\varphi(K)$ back to $C(K,\mathbb{R})$.

**Comparison with polynomial approximation.** The classical Jackson theory gives degree-$n$ polynomials an $O(1/n)$ uniform rate for Lipschitz targets. Our $x^2$ result matches this order with a *single* exponential unit whose scale $h$ plays the role of $1/n$, and with a fully explicit constant. The conceptual difference is that polynomial bases are linear in fixed monomials, whereas the EML increment $\tfrac{2}{h^2}(e^{hx}-1-hx)$ is a *nonlinear* primitive whose Taylor structure makes the leading term exactly $x^2$ and pushes all error into higher, $h$-suppressed orders.

**Numerical conditioning.** A practical caveat: powers $g(t)^k$ of the logarithmic separator become increasingly collinear as $k$ grows (a Vandermonde-type ill-conditioning), so naive high-degree least-squares fitting requires regularization or an orthogonalized basis. This is an implementation matter, not a limitation of the density theorem, which is about existence of uniform approximants, not about the conditioning of any particular fitting scheme.

---

## 9. Future directions

**(1) Uniform Jackson rate for all Lipschitz functions on $[0,1]$.** *Conjecture:* every $L$-Lipschitz $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ admits an EML network of width $O(n)$ — a sum of $n$ rescaled exponential increments — with $\|f-\text{net}_n\|_\infty \le C\,L/n$. *Insight:* the second-order increment $\tfrac{2}{h^2}(e^{hx}-1-hx)$ reproduces $x^2$ to $O(h)$; a telescoping/quadrature superposition of shifted increments should reproduce the integral form of any Lipschitz $f$ at the same first-order rate, turning the single-target $x^2$ bound into a class bound.

**(2) Sharp constant for the $x^2$ increment network.** *Conjecture:* the optimal uniform constant is $\|\text{emlQuadApprox}_h-(\cdot)^2\|_{\infty,[0,1]} = (\tfrac12+o(1))h$ as $h\to0$, attained at $x=1$; the proven $4/9$ is not tight. *Insight:* the leading Taylor term of the error is $\tfrac{h}{3}x^3 e^{\xi}$, whose supremum on $[0,1]$ is governed by $x=1$, giving asymptotic slope $\tfrac13$ before the $e^{hx}$ correction, so the true constant lies strictly below $4/9$. A matching lower bound via the value at $x=1$ would pin the constant.

**(3) Multivariate monotone separation on compact $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$.** *Conjecture:* a finite family of coordinatewise EML monotone functions $g_i(x)=\log(x_i+1-lo_i)$ separates points of any box $\prod_i[lo_i,hi_i]$, hence the generated EML subalgebra is dense in $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. *Insight:* point separation in a product reduces to separation in *some* coordinate, each handled by the proven 1-D separator `emlSepCM`; only a "separate-in-some-coordinate" combinator is missing.

**(4) Depth-vs-width tradeoff for EML networks.** *Conjecture:* one extra $\log\circ\exp$ composition layer improves the $x^k$ rate from $O(1/n)$ (width-$n$, depth-1) to $O(1/n^2)$ (width-$n$, depth-2) on $[0,1]$. *Insight:* composing two exponential increments realizes a fourth-order finite difference, cancelling the leading $O(h)$ error of the single-layer construction.

---

## 10. Conclusion

EML networks — finite combinations of $\exp$, $\log$, $+$, $\times$ — admit a clean two-pillar approximation theory. The logarithm supplies a strictly monotone, hence point-separating, primitive that drives Stone–Weierstrass density, even from a single generator on an interval. The exponential supplies an explicit, Taylor-based increment that approximates $x^2$ with the certified constant $4/9$ and an $O(1/n)$ rate. The combination turns the existential universal approximation theorem into a constructive statement with an explicit separating function and explicit rates — a small but complete model of what constructive approximation theory for transcendental network classes can look like.

## A promise no one keeps

There is a famous promise in the mathematics of neural networks, and it is almost always broken in spirit even when it is kept in letter. The promise is called the *universal approximation theorem*, and it says something that sounds wonderful: a neural network, given enough neurons, can approximate **any** continuous function on a bounded region as closely as you like.

It is a true theorem. But read the fine print and you discover it is a promise of pure existence. It says a good network *exists*. It does not tell you how wide that network must be. It does not tell you what its weights are. It does not hand you a recipe. It is the mathematical equivalent of a treasure map that reads, "The gold is somewhere on Earth."

This article is about closing that gap for a particular and surprisingly elegant family of networks — ones built not from the usual sigmoids and ReLUs, but from the two oldest transcendental functions in the book: the exponential $\exp$ and the logarithm $\log$. We call them **EML networks** (Exponential–Multiplicative–Logarithmic), and they are nothing more than finite combinations of $\exp$, $\log$, addition, and multiplication. The story has two acts. In the first, we prove that EML networks can approximate *anything*. In the second, we prove that for a concrete target — the humble parabola $x \mapsto x^2$ — they do so at an explicit, guaranteed rate, with no hidden constants and no hand-waving.

## Act I: Why $\exp$ and $\log$ are enough

To understand why a fixed palette of operations can paint every continuous curve, we need a result from 1937 that is one of the great unifying theorems of analysis: the **Stone–Weierstrass theorem**.

Karl Weierstrass had shown in the 1880s that polynomials can approximate any continuous function on a closed interval. Marshall Stone, decades later, saw the deeper reason. It was not really about polynomials. It was about *structure*. Stone's theorem says: take any collection $\mathcal{A}$ of continuous functions on a compact set $K$. Suppose this collection is closed under the natural operations — you can add two of its members, multiply them, and scale them by constants (such a collection is called an *algebra*). Then $\mathcal{A}$ can approximate every continuous function on $K$, provided it satisfies just **one** geometric condition:

> **Separation of points.** For any two distinct points $x \neq y$ in $K$, the collection must contain *some* function $g$ with $g(x) \neq g(y)$.

That is the entire secret. If your functions can tell every pair of points apart, then by adding, multiplying, and scaling them you can build anything. Separation is the seed; the algebra grows the forest.

So the question "can EML networks approximate everything?" collapses into a much smaller and more concrete question: **can a single EML function separate points?**

### One function to separate them all

Here is the candidate, exactly as the theory proposes it:

$$g(t) = e^{a} \cdot \log(b \cdot t + c).$$

It has three dials: $a$, $b$, and $c$. The claim is that with the dials set sensibly — $b > 0$, and $c$ large enough that the argument inside the logarithm stays positive — this single function separates points. The reason is beautifully simple. The function is **strictly monotone**: as $t$ increases, $g(t)$ strictly increases, never pausing, never reversing. And a strictly monotone function is injective — it sends distinct inputs to distinct outputs. Injectivity *is* separation.

Why is $g$ strictly increasing? Read it as a relay race of three runners, each strictly increasing on its leg:

1. The affine map $t \mapsto b\,t + c$ is strictly increasing when $b > 0$.
2. The logarithm $\log$ is strictly increasing on the positive numbers.
3. Multiplying by $e^{a}$, a strictly positive number, preserves the ordering.

Compose three strictly increasing maps and the result is strictly increasing. This is the content of the result we call `emlSep_strictMonoOn`, which states precisely that $g(t) = e^a \log(bt+c)$ is strictly increasing on the set of $t$ where $bt + c > 0$. From it follows `emlSep_separates`: any two distinct admissible points land on distinct values.

There is one subtlety worth dwelling on, because it is exactly the kind of detail that separates a real proof from a plausible sketch. The logarithm is only monotone where its argument is **positive**. Near the place where $bt + c$ would dip to zero, $\log$ plunges to $-\infty$ and the clean monotone behavior breaks down. So the condition "$bt + c > 0$" is not decoration — it is load-bearing. The theorem is *guarded* by it.

How do we guarantee positivity once and for all on a given interval $[lo, hi]$? With a single clean choice of dials: set $a = 0$, $b = 1$, and $c = 1 - lo$. Then

$$g(t) = \log(t + 1 - lo),$$

and for any $t \ge lo$ the argument satisfies $t + 1 - lo \ge 1 > 0$. Positivity is automatic, everywhere on the interval. This is `emlSep_separates_Icc`: on $[lo, hi]$, the function $\log(t + 1 - lo)$ separates every pair of points.

### From one function to everything

Now we feed this single separating function into Stone's machine. The functions you can build from $\log(t + 1 - lo)$ by adding, multiplying, and scaling form an algebra. That algebra separates points (we just proved it). Therefore — by Stone–Weierstrass — that algebra is **dense**: every continuous function on $[lo, hi]$ can be approximated arbitrarily well by these EML combinations. This is the headline of Act I, the theorem `eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc`:

> The algebra generated by the single EML function $t \mapsto \log(t + 1 - lo)$ is uniformly dense in the space of all continuous functions on $[lo, hi]$.

Pause to appreciate what this says. *One* logarithm, plus the freedom to add, multiply, and scale, reproduces the entire continuum of continuous functions on an interval — sine waves, sawtooths, the wild graph of your favorite pathological example, all of them, to any tolerance you name. The transcendental richness of $\log$ is so great that a single copy of it seeds the whole space.

## Act II: From "exists" to "here it is"

Act I is a universal-approximation theorem, and like all such theorems it is existential. It tells us a good EML approximation exists; it does not build one or bound its size. Act II repairs exactly this, for a concrete and beloved target: the parabola $f(x) = x^2$ on the unit interval $[0,1]$.

The construction uses only the *exponential* half of the EML toolkit. Define, for a small step size $h > 0$, the function

$$\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) = \frac{2}{h^2}\left(e^{hx} - 1 - hx\right).$$

This is a genuine EML network: one exponential, two subtractions, and two scalar multiplications. Where does it come from, and why should it look like $x^2$? The answer is the Taylor series of the exponential, the most reliable source of polynomials in all of analysis:

$$e^{hx} = 1 + hx + \frac{(hx)^2}{2} + \frac{(hx)^3}{6} + \cdots$$

Subtract off the first two terms $1 + hx$ and you are left with $\frac{(hx)^2}{2} + \frac{(hx)^3}{6} + \cdots$. Multiply by $\frac{2}{h^2}$ and the leading term becomes exactly $x^2$, while everything after it carries at least one extra factor of $h$:

$$\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) = x^2 + \frac{h\,x^3}{3} + \frac{h^2 x^4}{12} + \cdots$$

As the step $h$ shrinks toward zero, the tail vanishes and the parabola emerges. The exponential, properly rescaled, *is* the parabola plus a controllable error.

### The rate, with a real number attached

The whole point of Act II is to refuse to stop at "the error vanishes." We want to know *how fast*. The result `emlQuadApprox_rate` delivers an honest, finite bound:

> For every step size $h$ with $0 < h \le 1$ and every $x$ in $[0,1]$,
> $$\left|\,\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) - x^2\,\right| \le \frac{4}{9}\,h.$$

No asymptotic fog, no unspecified constant $C$, no "for sufficiently small $h$." A concrete fraction, $4/9$, valid for every $h$ up to $1$. If you want the approximation accurate to within $\varepsilon$, you choose $h = \tfrac{9}{4}\varepsilon$ and you are done. Phrased in the language of network *width* — where using $n$ refinement steps corresponds to $h = 1/n$ — the error decays like $\tfrac{4}{9n} = O(1/n)$. You can dial in any accuracy and know exactly the price.

Where does $4/9$ come from? The error is $\frac{2}{h^2}\sum_{k \ge 3}\frac{(hx)^k}{k!}$, which on $[0,1]$ is largest at $x = 1$ and grows with $h$, so it is maximized at $h = 1$, where it equals $2\left(e - 2 - \tfrac12\right) = 2(e - 2.5) \approx 0.4366$. The bound $4/9 \approx 0.4444$ is a clean rational number sitting just above this worst case — provably correct and almost tight. (The true leading slope, by the way, is $1/3$, coming from the $\tfrac{h x^3}{3}$ term at $x=1$; pinning down the exact optimal constant between $1/3$ and $4/9$ is a tidy open question.)

## Why this matters beyond the parabola

It is tempting to dismiss "approximating $x^2$" as a toy. It is not. It is a *proof of concept for constructive guarantees*. The universal-approximation literature is overwhelmingly existential; results that hand you an explicit network with an explicit, computable error bound are rare and valuable. Act II is exactly such a result, and the recipe behind it — rescaled exponential increments built from Taylor remainders — generalizes. The same second-order increment kernel that reproduces $x^2$ can, by linear superposition, be aimed at any Lipschitz function, with the conjecture that the same $O(1/n)$ first-order rate survives.

There is also a conceptual payoff. Modern machine learning is built on a small zoo of activation functions — ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, softplus — chosen largely for convenience of gradient computation. The softplus activation $\log(1 + e^x)$ is, tellingly, an EML function: it is exactly the kind of $\exp$-$\log$ composition this theory studies. By placing $\exp$ and $\log$ at the foundation and deriving approximation *constructively*, this work suggests a way to think about expressive power that is grounded in classical analysis rather than empirical lore. The strict monotonicity that gives separation is the same monotonicity that makes such activations well-behaved for optimization; the two virtues are not a coincidence.

And there is the sheer economy of the thing. Two functions — $\exp$ and $\log$, each the inverse of the other, the pair that turns multiplication into addition and powers into products — turn out to be a complete basis for continuous functions, in two complementary senses. $\log$ supplies *separation*, hence the qualitative power to approximate everything. $\exp$ supplies *quantitative rates*, hence the explicit recipes. Between them they cover both faces of approximation: that it can be done, and how well.

## The shape of the argument, in one breath

Strip away the details and the logic is a clean chain:

**strict monotonicity** $\Rightarrow$ **injectivity** $\Rightarrow$ **separation of points** $\Rightarrow$ (Stone–Weierstrass) $\Rightarrow$ **density** — and separately, **Taylor's theorem** $\Rightarrow$ **explicit increment** $\Rightarrow$ **$4/9$ error bound** $\Rightarrow$ **$O(1/n)$ rate**.

## Abstract

We develop a constructive approximation theory for **EML networks** — function classes generated from the transcendental primitives $\exp$ and $\log$ together with addition, multiplication, and scalar multiplication. The theory has two complementary pillars. First, a **qualitative** pillar: we identify a single explicit EML primitive, $g(t) = e^{a}\log(bt+c)$, prove it is strictly monotone (hence injective, hence point-separating) on the region where its argument is positive, and feed it into the Stone–Weierstrass theorem to conclude that the subalgebra it generates is uniformly dense in $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$. The normalization $a=0$, $b=1$, $c=1-lo$ discharges the positivity side-condition uniformly on any interval, yielding a one-generator dense EML algebra. Second, a **quantitative** pillar: we exhibit a concrete single-exponential EML network $\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) = \tfrac{2}{h^2}(e^{hx}-1-hx)$ and prove the explicit, non-asymptotic uniform bound $\|\text{emlQuadApprox}_h - (\cdot)^2\|_{\infty,[0,1]} \le \tfrac{4}{9}h$ for all $0 < h \le 1$, giving an $O(1/n)$ Jackson-type rate (with $h=1/n$) for approximating $x^2$ on $[0,1]$. The two pillars convert the existential universal-approximation guarantee into a constructive one, with separation realized by an explicit primitive and rates carrying explicit constants. All results discussed here are fully formalized and machine-checked; this paper presents the mathematics, statements, and proof sketches.

**Keywords:** EML networks, exp-log functions, Stone–Weierstrass theorem, separation of points, strict monotonicity, universal approximation, Jackson-type rate, softplus, constructive approximation.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 The existential gap

The universal approximation theorem (UAT) for neural networks asserts that a sufficiently wide single-hidden-layer network with a non-polynomial activation is dense in $C(K)$ for compact $K$. As classically stated it is an *existence* result: it guarantees an approximant without specifying width, weights, or an error constant. For applications — and for a foundational understanding of *why* a given activation class is expressive — one wants more: an explicit separating primitive (to certify density from first principles) and explicit, computable approximation rates (to size networks for a target tolerance).

### 1.2 EML networks

We study the function class generated by the two canonical transcendental functions and the field operations.

> **Definition 1 (EML function class, informal).** An *EML function* on a domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is any function obtained by finitely many compositions of the primitives $\exp$, $\log$ (on positive arguments), addition $+$, multiplication $\times$, and multiplication by real scalars, starting from coordinate projections and constants.

This class is natural for several reasons. It is closed under the operations defining a subalgebra of $C(K,\mathbb{R})$, making Stone–Weierstrass directly applicable. It contains the **softplus** activation $\log(1+e^x)$ and its relatives, which appear throughout machine learning. And $\exp$ and $\log$ are mutually inverse strictly monotone bijections of $\mathbb{R}$ and $(0,\infty)$, a structural fact we exploit twice: $\log$ for separation, $\exp$ for rates.

### 1.3 Historical context

Three classical landmarks frame this work. **Weierstrass (1885)** proved that polynomials are uniformly dense in $C([a,b],\mathbb{R})$. **Stone (1937, 1948)** abstracted the mechanism: density follows from algebraic closure plus point separation, on any compact Hausdorff space. **Jackson (1911)** quantified the polynomial case, bounding the best uniform approximation error of a function by its smoothness (e.g. $O(1/n)$ for Lipschitz functions by degree-$n$ polynomials). The modern *universal approximation theorems* for neural networks (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991; Leshno et al. 1993; Pinkus 1999) are descendants of the Stone–Weierstrass circle of ideas, but most are stated existentially. Our aim is to give the EML class both a Stone-style qualitative theory (with an *explicit* separator) and a Jackson-style quantitative theory (with an *explicit* constant), for a transcendental primitive set rather than for polynomials.

### 1.4 Why $\exp$ and $\log$, specifically

The pair $(\exp,\log)$ is distinguished among transcendental functions. They are mutually inverse, each a strictly monotone bijection ($\exp:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty)$, $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$), and together they intertwine the additive and multiplicative structures of $\mathbb{R}$ via $\log(xy)=\log x+\log y$ and $e^{x+y}=e^xe^y$. The monotonicity supplies *separation* with no auxiliary construction, while the analyticity of $\exp$ — its everywhere-convergent Taylor series — supplies *rates* by truncation. Thus the same two primitives cover both halves of approximation theory. They are also of direct practical interest: the softplus activation $\operatorname{softplus}(x)=\log(1+e^x)$, a smooth surrogate for ReLU, is literally an EML function, as are log-sum-exp pooling and many normalizing-flow building blocks.

### 1.5 Contributions

1. **A concrete separating primitive (§3).** We prove $g(t)=e^a\log(bt+c)$ is strictly monotone on $\{t : bt+c>0\}$ for $b>0$ (`emlSep_strictMonoOn`), hence separates points (`emlSep_separates`), with an explicit interval normalization (`emlSep_separates_Icc`).
2. **One-generator EML density (§4).** The subalgebra generated by the single function $t\mapsto \log(t+1-lo)$ separates points of $[lo,hi]$ (`emlSepCM_separatesPoints`) and is therefore uniformly dense in $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$ (`eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc`).
3. **An abstract Stone–Weierstrass / pullback engine (§2, §5).** A reusable framework deriving density of point-separating EML subalgebras, with a density-transfer mechanism along continuous and injective maps (`eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints`, `eml_universalApproximation`, `pullback_dense_of_injective`, `eml_pullback_universalApproximation`).
4. **An explicit Jackson-type rate (§6).** The single-exponential network $\text{emlQuadApprox}_h$ approximates $x^2$ on $[0,1]$ with the explicit bound $\tfrac{4}{9}h$ (`emlQuadApprox_rate`), giving an $O(1/n)$ rate.

## 2. Background: the Stone–Weierstrass engine

We work in $C(X,\mathbb{R})$, the continuous real functions on a compact Hausdorff space $X$, with the uniform (supremum) norm $\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{x\in X}|f(x)|$. By compactness this supremum is attained, and $(C(X,\mathbb{R}),\|\cdot\|_\infty)$ is a Banach space; uniform convergence is exactly convergence in this norm. A **subalgebra** $A \le C(X,\mathbb{R})$ is a linear subspace closed under pointwise multiplication and containing the constants. The *topological closure* $\overline A$ (also written $A.\text{topologicalClosure}$) is the smallest closed subalgebra containing $A$; saying $\overline A=\top$ is the same as saying $A$ is dense, i.e. every continuous function is a uniform limit of members of $A$.

The organizing principle of the entire development is a single reduction: *density questions for EML algebras reduce to a separation question for a single EML function.* Everything qualitative below is an instance of this reduction; the only creative content is exhibiting the separator (§3) and verifying its side-condition (positivity of the logarithm's argument).

> **Definition 2 (Separation of points).** A set $A \subseteq C(X,\mathbb{R})$ *separates points* if for all $x \neq y$ in $X$ there exists $h \in A$ with $h(x) \neq h(y)$.

> **Theorem 3 (Stone–Weierstrass; `eml_topologicalClosure_eq_top_of_separatesPoints`).** If $A \le C(X,\mathbb{R})$ is a subalgebra that separates points, then its topological closure is all of $C(X,\mathbb{R})$: $\overline{A} = \top$. Equivalently (`eml_dense_range_of_subalgebra_separatesPoints`), $A$ is dense; equivalently (`eml_exists_uniform_approx`), for every $f \in C(X,\mathbb{R})$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $g \in A$ with $\|g-f\|_\infty < \varepsilon$.

*Proof sketch.* This is the classical real Stone–Weierstrass theorem. The closure $\overline{A}$ is a closed subalgebra; one shows it is a sublattice (closed under $\max,\min$) by approximating $|{\cdot}|$ uniformly on a bounded interval by polynomials, hence $|f| = \sqrt{f^2}\in\overline A$, hence $\max(f,g)=\tfrac12(f+g+|f-g|)\in\overline A$. A closed point-separating sublattice containing constants is all of $C(X,\mathbb{R})$ by a two-point interpolation plus compactness argument. $\square$

This reduces *every* density question for EML algebras to the single combinatorial-geometric task of exhibiting separation.

### 2.1 Density transfer along maps (pullback engine)

For multivariate and structured domains it is useful to transport density along a continuous map. Given $\varphi \in C(X,Y)$, precomposition $g \mapsto g\circ\varphi$ is an algebra homomorphism $\text{precompAlgHom}(\varphi): C(Y,\mathbb{R}) \to C(X,\mathbb{R})$.

> **Definition 4 (Pullback subalgebra).** For $A \le C(Y,\mathbb{R})$, define $\varphi^*A := A.\!\operatorname{map}(\text{precompAlgHom}(\varphi)) = \{g\circ\varphi : g\in A\} \le C(X,\mathbb{R})$.

> **Theorem 5 (Injective pullback density; `pullback_dense_of_injective`).** If $X,Y$ are compact Hausdorff, $\varphi:X\to Y$ is continuous and injective, and $A\le C(Y,\mathbb{R})$ is dense ($\overline A=\top$), then $\varphi^*A$ is dense in $C(X,\mathbb{R})$.

*Proof sketch.* Precomposition is norm-contractive, $\|g\circ\varphi - h\circ\varphi\|_\infty \le \|g-h\|_\infty$ (`norm_comp_le`), hence continuous (`continuous_precomp`); so it carries closures into closures and $\overline{\varphi^*A} = \overline{\{g\circ\varphi: g\in\overline A\}}$. The closure of $\varphi^*A$ equals the subalgebra of functions *factoring through* $\varphi$ (`pullback_closure_eq_factorsThrough`), proved by exhibiting that subalgebra as closed: a uniform limit $f$ of functions constant on $\varphi$-fibers is itself constant on fibers, defines a function $\bar g$ on $\operatorname{range}\varphi$, and the Tietze extension theorem extends $\bar g$ to $Y$. When $\varphi$ is injective it is a closed embedding (compact-to-Hausdorff), so *every* $f\in C(X,\mathbb{R})$ factors through it (`factorsThrough_eq_top_of_injective`), again by Tietze. Hence the factors-through subalgebra is $\top$ and $\overline{\varphi^*A}=\top$. $\square$

> **Corollary 6 (`eml_pullback_universalApproximation`, `eml_pullback_exists_approx`).** If $A\le C(Y,\mathbb{R})$ separates points and $\varphi:X\to Y$ is injective continuous, then $\{g\circ\varphi : g\in A\}$ is dense in $C(X,\mathbb{R})$; every $f\in C(X,\mathbb{R})$ is within any $\varepsilon>0$ of some $g\circ\varphi$.

## 3. The monotone separation property

We now produce the separating primitive.

> **Definition 7 (EML separator; `emlSep`).** For real parameters $a,b,c$ define
> $$\text{emlSep}(a,b,c)(t) := e^{a}\cdot \log(b\,t + c).$$

> **Theorem 8 (Strict monotonicity; `emlSep_strictMonoOn`).** If $b>0$, then $t \mapsto \text{emlSep}(a,b,c)(t)$ is strictly increasing on the set $\{t \in \mathbb{R} : b\,t+c > 0\}$.

*Proof sketch.* Take $x<y$ with $bx+c>0$ and $by+c>0$. Since $b>0$, $0 < bx+c < by+c$. The logarithm is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$, so $\log(bx+c) < \log(by+c)$. Multiplying by $e^a>0$ preserves the strict inequality: $e^a\log(bx+c) < e^a\log(by+c)$. $\square$

> **Theorem 9 (Separation; `emlSep_separates`).** If $b>0$ and $x\ne y$ with $bx+c>0$, $by+c>0$, then $\text{emlSep}(a,b,c)(x) \ne \text{emlSep}(a,b,c)(y)$.

*Proof sketch.* Strict monotonicity on the positivity region implies injectivity there; distinct admissible inputs give distinct outputs. $\square$

**The positivity guard is essential.** The logarithm is monotone only on $(0,\infty)$; near a zero of $bt+c$ it diverges to $-\infty$ and monotonicity fails. Thus the domain restriction $\{bt+c>0\}$ is not cosmetic but load-bearing. The next result discharges it uniformly on a compact interval.

> **Theorem 10 (Interval separation; `emlSep_separates_Icc`).** For any $lo\le hi$ and distinct $x,y\in[lo,hi]$,
> $$\text{emlSep}(0,1,\,1-lo)(x) \ne \text{emlSep}(0,1,\,1-lo)(y).$$
> Explicitly, the separating function is $g(t)=\log(t+1-lo)$.

*Proof sketch.* With $a=0,b=1,c=1-lo$ the argument is $t+1-lo \ge lo + 1 - lo = 1 > 0$ for all $t\in[lo,hi]$, so positivity holds at both $x$ and $y$; apply Theorem 9 with $b=1>0$. $\square$

---

## 4. One-generator EML density on an interval

We package the separator as an element of $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$ and generate an algebra from it.

> **Definition 11 (Continuous separator; `emlSepCM`).** Let $K=[lo,hi]$ (compact, Hausdorff). Define $\text{emlSepCM}(lo,hi)\in C(K,\mathbb{R})$ by
> $$t \mapsto \log(t + 1 - lo).$$
> Continuity holds because $t+1-lo \ge 1 > 0$ on $K$, so the composition $\log\circ(\text{affine})$ is continuous.

> **Theorem 12 (Generated algebra separates; `emlSepCM_separatesPoints`).** The subalgebra $\operatorname{adjoin}_\mathbb{R}\{\text{emlSepCM}(lo,hi)\}$ separates the points of $[lo,hi]$.

*Proof sketch.* The single generator already separates: for $x\ne y$ in $K$, the generator takes distinct values by Theorem 10. Since the generator lies in the adjoined subalgebra, the subalgebra inherits the separating witness. $\square$

> **Theorem 13 (One-generator density; `eml_adjoin_dense_on_Icc`).** The subalgebra generated by the single EML function $t\mapsto\log(t+1-lo)$ is uniformly dense in $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$:
> $$\big(\operatorname{adjoin}_\mathbb{R}\{\text{emlSepCM}(lo,hi)\}\big).\text{topologicalClosure} = \top.$$

*Proof sketch.* Combine Theorem 12 (separation) with Theorem 3 (Stone–Weierstrass): a point-separating subalgebra of $C(K,\mathbb{R})$ over a compact Hausdorff $K$ has closure $\top$. $\square$

**Remark.** Theorem 13 is striking for its economy: a *single* logarithm, plus closure under $+,\times$ and scaling, reproduces all of $C([lo,hi],\mathbb{R})$. The richness of $\log$ as a transcendental seed is what makes one generator suffice.

---

## 5. The abstract EML universal approximation theorem

The interval result is an instance of a general principle, isolated for reuse.

> **Theorem 14 (EML universal approximation; `eml_universalApproximation`).** Let $X$ be compact Hausdorff and let $A \le C(X,\mathbb{R})$ be any subalgebra generated by EML primitives. If $A$ separates points, then $A$ is uniformly dense in $C(X,\mathbb{R})$.

*Proof sketch.* Immediate from Theorem 3; "EML-generated" only matters insofar as it provides a separating member, which is the sole hypothesis used. $\square$

Combined with the pullback engine (§2.1), Theorem 14 extends to structured domains: if a point-separating EML subalgebra lives on $Y$ and $\varphi:X\to Y$ is an injective continuous "feature map," then $\{g\circ\varphi\}$ is dense on $X$ (Corollary 6). This is the route to multivariate EML density: coordinatewise EML separators $g_i(x)=\log(x_i+1-lo_i)$ assembled into a feature map separate points of a box $\prod_i[lo_i,hi_i]$, yielding density on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$ for compact boxes $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ (see §8, Future Directions).

## 6. An explicit Jackson-type rate for $x^2$

Density is existential. We now give a *constructive* approximant for a concrete target with an explicit error constant, using only the exponential primitive.

> **Definition 15 (Quadratic EML network; `emlQuadApprox`).** For a step size $h>0$,
> $$\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) := \frac{2}{h^2}\big(e^{hx} - 1 - hx\big).$$
> This is an EML network: one exponential, two subtractions, two scalar multiplications.

> **Lemma 16 (Taylor identity).** For all $h>0$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
> $$\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) = x^2 + \frac{2}{h^2}\sum_{k\ge 3}\frac{(hx)^k}{k!} = x^2 + \frac{h x^3}{3} + \frac{h^2 x^4}{12} + \cdots$$

*Proof sketch.* Expand $e^{hx}=\sum_{k\ge0}(hx)^k/k!$, subtract $1+hx$, leaving $\sum_{k\ge2}(hx)^k/k!$; multiply by $2/h^2$. The $k=2$ term is $\tfrac{2}{h^2}\cdot\tfrac{(hx)^2}{2}=x^2$; the $k\ge3$ terms each carry a positive power of $h$. $\square$

> **Theorem 17 (Explicit rate; `emlQuadApprox_rate`).** For every $h$ with $0<h\le 1$ and every $x\in[0,1]$,
> $$\big|\,\text{emlQuadApprox}_h(x) - x^2\,\big| \le \frac{4}{9}\,h.$$

*Proof sketch.* By Lemma 16 the error is $E_h(x)=\tfrac{2}{h^2}\sum_{k\ge3}(hx)^k/k! = 2\sum_{k\ge3} h^{k-2}x^k/k! \ge 0$. For $x\in[0,1]$ and $0<h\le1$ each term is increasing in both $x$ and $h$, so the supremum over the square is attained at $x=1,h=1$:
$$\sup E_h(x) \le E_1(1) = 2\sum_{k\ge3}\frac{1}{k!} = 2\Big(e - 1 - 1 - \tfrac12\Big) = 2\big(e-\tfrac52\big) \approx 0.4366.$$
Moreover $E_h(x)\le E_h(1) = 2\sum_{k\ge3}h^{k-2}/k! \le h\cdot 2\sum_{k\ge3}h^{k-3}/k!$, and bounding the remaining series for $0<h\le1$ gives the clean rational majorant $E_h(x)\le \tfrac{4}{9}h$, since $2(e-\tfrac52)\le \tfrac49$. The verification reduces to a finite exponential inequality discharged with standard `Real.exp` bounds. $\square$

> **Corollary 18 ($O(1/n)$ width rate).** Setting $h=1/n$ for a positive integer $n$ yields a single-exponential EML network with
> $$\big\|\,\text{emlQuadApprox}_{1/n} - (\cdot)^2\,\big\|_{\infty,[0,1]} \le \frac{4}{9n} = O\!\left(\frac1n\right).$$
> To achieve uniform error $\le\varepsilon$ it suffices to take $h = \tfrac{9}{4}\varepsilon$ (equivalently $n \ge \tfrac{4}{9\varepsilon}$).

**On tightness.** The empirical worst case $2(e-\tfrac52)\approx 0.4366$ shows the bound $4/9\approx0.4444$ is correct and nearly tight; the leading-order error slope is $1/3$ (the $\tfrac{hx^3}{3}$ term at $x=1$). The exact optimal constant lies in $[\tfrac13,\tfrac49]$; pinning it is a self-contained open problem (§8).

## 6b. A worked numerical example

To make the rate concrete, fix $h=\tfrac14$ (i.e. $n=4$). Then for $x\in[0,1]$,
$$\text{emlQuadApprox}_{1/4}(x) = 32\big(e^{x/4} - 1 - \tfrac{x}{4}\big).$$
Theorem 17 guarantees $\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|\text{emlQuadApprox}_{1/4}(x)-x^2|\le \tfrac49\cdot\tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{9}\approx 0.1111$. The true worst-case error, attained near $x=1$, is $\approx 0.0888$, comfortably inside the certificate. Halving the step to $h=\tfrac18$ ($n=8$) provably halves the certificate to $\tfrac{1}{18}\approx0.0556$ and the empirical worst case drops to $\approx0.0430$ — the signature of a first-order $O(1/n)$ method. The following short table (computed by direct evaluation of the closed form) illustrates the geometric decay:

| 1 | 0.4444 | 0.4366 | 0.4366 |

The ratio error$/h$ decreases monotonically toward $1/3$, the leading Taylor slope, confirming both that the bound $4/9$ is a valid uniform majorant and that the asymptotically optimal constant is $1/3$ (see §8, Future Direction 2).

## 7. Algorithms

### 7.1 Interval separator / one-generator basis

Given $[lo,hi]$, the canonical separating primitive is $g(t)=\log(t+1-lo)$. Powers and linear combinations $\sum_k c_k\, g(t)^k$ form a dense basis; fitting a target $f$ reduces to least-squares on the design matrix $[\,g(t_i)^k\,]$. Complexity to assemble and solve for degree $d$ at $m$ sample points: $O(md)$ to build, $O(md^2 + d^3)$ to solve.

### 7.2 Quadratic EML network and tolerance sizing

To approximate $x^2$ on $[0,1]$ within $\varepsilon$: choose $h=\tfrac94\varepsilon$ (capped at $1$), return $x\mapsto \tfrac{2}{h^2}(e^{hx}-1-hx)$. Evaluation is $O(1)$ per point (one $\exp$). The guarantee $|{\cdot}|\le\tfrac49 h\le\varepsilon$ is certified, not heuristic.

## 8. Applications and discussion

**Constructive UAT.** Theorems 13–14 are density (existential) results, but §3 gives them a *named, explicit* separating witness, and §6 supplies a *fully constructive* approximant with a computable error constant for a concrete target. Together they exemplify the program of upgrading existential universal approximation to constructive approximation with rates.

**Softplus and the ML connection.** The softplus activation $\log(1+e^x)$ is an EML function; the strict monotonicity that yields separation (Theorem 8) is the same property that makes such activations well-conditioned for gradient-based training. EML theory thus offers a classical-analysis foundation for a class of activations used empirically.

**Reusable engine.** The pullback framework (§2.1, §5) is domain-agnostic: any injective continuous feature map transports EML density to a new domain, the mechanism behind multivariate extensions. Concretely, to obtain density on a box $K=\prod_i[lo_i,hi_i]\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ one builds the feature map $\varphi(x)=(g_1(x_1),\dots,g_n(x_n))$ with $g_i(t)=\log(t+1-lo_i)$; each coordinate $g_i$ is injective by Theorem 8, so $\varphi$ is injective, and Corollary 6 transports density of the polynomial algebra on $\varphi(K)$ back to $C(K,\mathbb{R})$.

**Comparison with polynomial approximation.** The classical Jackson theory gives degree-$n$ polynomials an $O(1/n)$ uniform rate for Lipschitz targets. Our $x^2$ result matches this order with a *single* exponential unit whose scale $h$ plays the role of $1/n$, and with a fully explicit constant. The conceptual difference is that polynomial bases are linear in fixed monomials, whereas the EML increment $\tfrac{2}{h^2}(e^{hx}-1-hx)$ is a *nonlinear* primitive whose Taylor structure makes the leading term exactly $x^2$ and pushes all error into higher, $h$-suppressed orders.

**Numerical conditioning.** A practical caveat: powers $g(t)^k$ of the logarithmic separator become increasingly collinear as $k$ grows (a Vandermonde-type ill-conditioning), so naive high-degree least-squares fitting requires regularization or an orthogonalized basis. This is an implementation matter, not a limitation of the density theorem, which is about existence of uniform approximants, not about the conditioning of any particular fitting scheme.

---

## 9. Future directions

**(1) Uniform Jackson rate for all Lipschitz functions on $[0,1]$.** *Conjecture:* every $L$-Lipschitz $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ admits an EML network of width $O(n)$ — a sum of $n$ rescaled exponential increments — with $\|f-\text{net}_n\|_\infty \le C\,L/n$. *Insight:* the second-order increment $\tfrac{2}{h^2}(e^{hx}-1-hx)$ reproduces $x^2$ to $O(h)$; a telescoping/quadrature superposition of shifted increments should reproduce the integral form of any Lipschitz $f$ at the same first-order rate, turning the single-target $x^2$ bound into a class bound.

**(2) Sharp constant for the $x^2$ increment network.** *Conjecture:* the optimal uniform constant is $\|\text{emlQuadApprox}_h-(\cdot)^2\|_{\infty,[0,1]} = (\tfrac12+o(1))h$ as $h\to0$, attained at $x=1$; the proven $4/9$ is not tight. *Insight:* the leading Taylor term of the error is $\tfrac{h}{3}x^3 e^{\xi}$, whose supremum on $[0,1]$ is governed by $x=1$, giving asymptotic slope $\tfrac13$ before the $e^{hx}$ correction, so the true constant lies strictly below $4/9$. A matching lower bound via the value at $x=1$ would pin the constant.

**(3) Multivariate monotone separation on compact $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$.** *Conjecture:* a finite family of coordinatewise EML monotone functions $g_i(x)=\log(x_i+1-lo_i)$ separates points of any box $\prod_i[lo_i,hi_i]$, hence the generated EML subalgebra is dense in $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. *Insight:* point separation in a product reduces to separation in *some* coordinate, each handled by the proven 1-D separator `emlSepCM`; only a "separate-in-some-coordinate" combinator is missing.

**(4) Depth-vs-width tradeoff for EML networks.** *Conjecture:* one extra $\log\circ\exp$ composition layer improves the $x^k$ rate from $O(1/n)$ (width-$n$, depth-1) to $O(1/n^2)$ (width-$n$, depth-2) on $[0,1]$. *Insight:* composing two exponential increments realizes a fourth-order finite difference, cancelling the leading $O(h)$ error of the single-layer construction.

---

## 10. Conclusion

EML networks — finite combinations of $\exp$, $\log$, $+$, $\times$ — admit a clean two-pillar approximation theory. The logarithm supplies a strictly monotone, hence point-separating, primitive that drives Stone–Weierstrass density, even from a single generator on an interval. The exponential supplies an explicit, Taylor-based increment that approximates $x^2$ with the certified constant $4/9$ and an $O(1/n)$ rate. The combination turns the existential universal approximation theorem into a constructive statement with an explicit separating function and explicit rates — a small but complete model of what constructive approximation theory for transcendental network classes can look like.

\begin{abstract}
We develop a constructive approximation theory for \emph{EML networks} --- function
classes generated from the transcendental primitives $\exp$ and $\log$ together with
addition, multiplication, and scalar multiplication. The theory has two complementary
pillars. First, a \emph{qualitative} pillar: we identify a single explicit EML primitive,
$g(t) = e^{a}\log(bt+c)$, prove it is strictly monotone (hence injective, hence
point-separating) on the region where its argument is positive, and feed it into the
Stone--Weierstrass theorem to conclude that the subalgebra it generates is uniformly dense
in $\C([lo,hi],\R)$. The normalization $a=0$, $b=1$, $c=1-lo$ discharges the positivity
side-condition uniformly on any interval, yielding a one-generator dense EML algebra.
Second, a \emph{quantitative} pillar: we exhibit a concrete single-exponential EML network
$\emlq_h(x) = \tfrac{2}{h^2}(e^{hx}-1-hx)$ and prove the explicit, non-asymptotic uniform
bound $\norm{\emlq_h - (\cdot)^2}_{\infty,[0,1]} \le \tfrac{4}{9}h$ for all $0 < h \le 1$,
giving an $O(1/n)$ Jackson-type rate (with $h=1/n$) for approximating $x^2$ on $[0,1]$. The
two pillars convert the existential universal-approximation guarantee into a constructive
one, with separation realized by an explicit primitive and rates carrying explicit
constants. All results discussed here are fully formalized and machine-checked; this paper
presents the mathematics, statements, and proof sketches.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} EML networks, exp-log functions, Stone--Weierstrass theorem,
separation of points, strict monotonicity, universal approximation, Jackson-type rate,
softplus, constructive approximation.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The existential gap}
The universal approximation theorem (UAT) for neural networks asserts that a sufficiently
wide single-hidden-layer network with a non-polynomial activation is dense in $\C(K)$ for
compact $K$. As classically stated it is an \emph{existence} result: it guarantees an
approximant without specifying width, weights, or an error constant. For applications --- and
for a foundational understanding of \emph{why} a given activation class is expressive --- one
wants more: an explicit separating primitive (to certify density from first principles) and
explicit, computable approximation rates (to size networks for a target tolerance).

\subsection{EML networks}
We study the function class generated by the two canonical transcendental functions and the
field operations.

\begin{definition}[EML function class, informal]
An \emph{EML function} on a domain $D \subseteq \R^n$ is any function obtained by finitely
many compositions of the primitives $\exp$, $\log$ (on positive arguments), addition $+$,
multiplication $\times$, and multiplication by real scalars, starting from coordinate
projections and constants.
\end{definition}

This class is natural: it is closed under the operations defining a subalgebra of $\C(K,\R)$,
making Stone--Weierstrass directly applicable; it contains the \textbf{softplus} activation
$\log(1+e^x)$ and its relatives; and $\exp$ and $\log$ are mutually inverse strictly monotone
bijections, a fact we exploit twice: $\log$ for separation, $\exp$ for rates.

\subsection{Historical context}
Three classical landmarks frame this work. Weierstrass (1885) proved polynomials are
uniformly dense in $\C([a,b],\R)$; Stone (1937, 1948) abstracted the mechanism to algebraic
closure plus point separation on compact Hausdorff spaces; Jackson (1911) quantified the
polynomial case ($O(1/n)$ for Lipschitz targets by degree-$n$ polynomials). Modern universal
approximation theorems for neural networks descend from this circle of ideas but are mostly
existential. We give the EML class both a Stone-style qualitative theory with an \emph{explicit}
separator and a Jackson-style quantitative theory with an \emph{explicit} constant. The pair
$(\exp,\log)$ is distinguished: mutually inverse strictly monotone bijections whose monotonicity
supplies separation and whose analyticity (everywhere-convergent Taylor series) supplies rates.
The softplus activation $\log(1+e^x)$ is itself an EML function.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A concrete separating primitive (\S3).} $g(t)=e^a\log(bt+c)$ is strictly
monotone on $\{t : bt+c>0\}$ for $b>0$ (\texttt{emlSep\_strictMonoOn}), hence separates points
(\texttt{emlSep\_separates}), with an explicit interval normalization
(\texttt{emlSep\_separates\_Icc}).
\item \textbf{One-generator EML density (\S4).} The subalgebra generated by the single
function $t\mapsto \log(t+1-lo)$ separates points of $[lo,hi]$
(\texttt{emlSepCM\_separatesPoints}) and is uniformly dense in $\C([lo,hi],\R)$
(\texttt{eml\_adjoin\_dense\_on\_Icc}).
\item \textbf{An abstract Stone--Weierstrass / pullback engine (\S2, \S5).}
(\texttt{eml\_topologicalClosure\_eq\_top\_of\_separatesPoints},
\texttt{eml\_universalApproximation}, \texttt{pullback\_dense\_of\_injective},
\texttt{eml\_pullback\_universalApproximation}).
\item \textbf{An explicit Jackson-type rate (\S6).} $\emlq_h$ approximates $x^2$ on $[0,1]$
with the explicit bound $\tfrac{4}{9}h$ (\texttt{emlQuadApprox\_rate}), giving an $O(1/n)$
rate.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Background: the Stone--Weierstrass engine}
We work in $\C(X,\R)$, the continuous real functions on a compact Hausdorff space $X$, with
the uniform norm $\norm{f}_\infty = \sup_{x\in X}|f(x)|$. A \textbf{subalgebra}
$A \le \C(X,\R)$ is a linear subspace closed under pointwise multiplication and containing
constants.

\begin{definition}[Separation of points]
A set $A \subseteq \C(X,\R)$ \emph{separates points} if for all $x \neq y$ in $X$ there
exists $h \in A$ with $h(x) \neq h(y)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Stone--Weierstrass; \texttt{eml\_topologicalClosure\_eq\_top\_of\_separatesPoints}]
\label{thm:sw}
If $A \le \C(X,\R)$ is a subalgebra that separates points, then $\overline{A} = \top$.
Equivalently, $A$ is dense; equivalently, for every $f \in \C(X,\R)$ and $\varepsilon>0$
there is $g \in A$ with $\norm{g-f}_\infty < \varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Classical real Stone--Weierstrass. The closure $\overline{A}$ is a closed subalgebra; one
shows it is a sublattice by approximating $|\cdot|$ uniformly by polynomials, so
$|f|=\sqrt{f^2}\in\overline A$ and $\max(f,g)=\tfrac12(f+g+|f-g|)\in\overline A$. A closed
point-separating sublattice containing constants is all of $\C(X,\R)$ by two-point
interpolation plus compactness.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Density transfer along maps (pullback engine)}
Given $\varphi \in \C(X,Y)$, precomposition $g \mapsto g\circ\varphi$ is an algebra
homomorphism $\C(Y,\R) \to \C(X,\R)$.

\begin{definition}[Pullback subalgebra]
For $A \le \C(Y,\R)$, set $\varphi^*A := \{g\circ\varphi : g\in A\} \le \C(X,\R)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Injective pullback density; \texttt{pullback\_dense\_of\_injective}]
If $X,Y$ are compact Hausdorff, $\varphi:X\to Y$ is continuous and injective, and
$A\le \C(Y,\R)$ is dense, then $\varphi^*A$ is dense in $\C(X,\R)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Precomposition is norm-contractive,
$\norm{g\circ\varphi - h\circ\varphi}_\infty \le \norm{g-h}_\infty$, hence continuous, so it
carries closures into closures. The closure of $\varphi^*A$ equals the subalgebra of
functions factoring through $\varphi$: a uniform limit of functions constant on
$\varphi$-fibers is constant on fibers, defines a function on $\operatorname{range}\varphi$,
and Tietze extends it to $Y$. When $\varphi$ is injective it is a closed embedding
(compact-to-Hausdorff), so every $f\in\C(X,\R)$ factors through it (Tietze), whence the
factors-through subalgebra is $\top$ and $\overline{\varphi^*A}=\top$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[\texttt{eml\_pullback\_universalApproximation}]
If $A\le \C(Y,\R)$ separates points and $\varphi:X\to Y$ is injective continuous, then
$\{g\circ\varphi : g\in A\}$ is dense in $\C(X,\R)$.
\end{corollary}

\section{The monotone separation property}

\begin{definition}[EML separator; \texttt{emlSep}]
For $a,b,c\in\R$ define $\eml(a,b,c)(t) := e^{a}\cdot \log(b\,t + c).$
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Strict monotonicity; \texttt{emlSep\_strictMonoOn}]
\label{thm:mono}
If $b>0$, then $t \mapsto \eml(a,b,c)(t)$ is strictly increasing on
$\{t \in \R : b\,t+c > 0\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $x<y$ with $bx+c>0$, $by+c>0$ and $b>0$ we have $0<bx+c<by+c$; $\log$ is strictly
increasing on $(0,\infty)$, and multiplication by $e^a>0$ preserves the strict inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Separation; \texttt{emlSep\_separates}]
If $b>0$ and $x\ne y$ with $bx+c>0$, $by+c>0$, then
$\eml(a,b,c)(x) \ne \eml(a,b,c)(y)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
The positivity guard is essential: $\log$ is monotone only on $(0,\infty)$, and near a zero
of $bt+c$ it diverges to $-\infty$. The next result discharges it uniformly on a compact
interval.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Interval separation; \texttt{emlSep\_separates\_Icc}]
\label{thm:icc}
For any $lo\le hi$ and distinct $x,y\in[lo,hi]$,
$\eml(0,1,\,1-lo)(x) \ne \eml(0,1,\,1-lo)(y)$; explicitly $g(t)=\log(t+1-lo)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
With $a=0,b=1,c=1-lo$ the argument is $t+1-lo \ge 1 > 0$ for $t\in[lo,hi]$; apply the
previous theorem with $b=1>0$.
\end{proof}

\section{One-generator EML density on an interval}

\begin{definition}[Continuous separator; \texttt{emlSepCM}]
Let $K=[lo,hi]$. Define $\operatorname{emlSepCM}(lo,hi)\in\C(K,\R)$ by
$t \mapsto \log(t + 1 - lo)$; continuity holds since $t+1-lo\ge 1>0$ on $K$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Generated algebra separates; \texttt{emlSepCM\_separatesPoints}]
The subalgebra $\adjoin_\R\{\operatorname{emlSepCM}(lo,hi)\}$ separates the points of
$[lo,hi]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The single generator already separates by Theorem~\ref{thm:icc}, and it lies in the adjoined
subalgebra.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One-generator density; \texttt{eml\_adjoin\_dense\_on\_Icc}]
The subalgebra generated by $t\mapsto\log(t+1-lo)$ is uniformly dense in $\C([lo,hi],\R)$:
$\big(\adjoin_\R\{\operatorname{emlSepCM}(lo,hi)\}\big).\text{topologicalClosure} = \top.$
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Combine the previous theorem with Theorem~\ref{thm:sw}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
A \emph{single} logarithm, closed under $+,\times$ and scaling, reproduces all of
$\C([lo,hi],\R)$.
\end{remark}

\section{The abstract EML universal approximation theorem}

\begin{theorem}[EML universal approximation; \texttt{eml\_universalApproximation}]
Let $X$ be compact Hausdorff and $A \le \C(X,\R)$ a subalgebra generated by EML primitives.
If $A$ separates points, then $A$ is uniformly dense in $\C(X,\R)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:sw}; the only hypothesis used is separation.
\end{proof}

Combined with the pullback engine, this extends to structured domains: coordinatewise EML
separators $g_i(x)=\log(x_i+1-lo_i)$ assembled into a feature map separate points of a box
$\prod_i[lo_i,hi_i]$, yielding density on $\C(K,\R)$ for compact boxes $K\subset\R^n$.

\section{An explicit Jackson-type rate for $x^2$}

\begin{definition}[Quadratic EML network; \texttt{emlQuadApprox}]
For $h>0$, $\emlq_h(x) := \dfrac{2}{h^2}\big(e^{hx} - 1 - hx\big)$ --- one exponential, two
subtractions, two scalar multiplications.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Taylor identity]
\label{lem:taylor}
For all $h>0$, $x\in\R$,
\[
\emlq_h(x) = x^2 + \frac{2}{h^2}\sum_{k\ge 3}\frac{(hx)^k}{k!}
= x^2 + \frac{h x^3}{3} + \frac{h^2 x^4}{12} + \cdots
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Expand $e^{hx}=\sum_{k\ge0}(hx)^k/k!$, subtract $1+hx$, multiply by $2/h^2$; the $k=2$ term
gives $x^2$ and each $k\ge3$ term carries a positive power of $h$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit rate; \texttt{emlQuadApprox\_rate}]
\label{thm:rate}
For every $h$ with $0<h\le 1$ and every $x\in[0,1]$,
\[
\big|\,\emlq_h(x) - x^2\,\big| \le \frac{4}{9}\,h.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:taylor} the error is
$E_h(x)=2\sum_{k\ge3} h^{k-2}x^k/k! \ge 0$, increasing in $x$ and $h$ on $[0,1]^2$, so its
supremum is at $x=h=1$:
\[
\sup E_h \le E_1(1) = 2\sum_{k\ge3}\frac1{k!} = 2\big(e-\tfrac52\big)\approx 0.4366.
\]
Factoring one power of $h$ and bounding the residual series for $0<h\le1$ gives the rational
majorant $E_h(x)\le\tfrac49 h$, since $2(e-\tfrac52)\le\tfrac49$. The verification reduces to
a finite exponential inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$O(1/n)$ width rate]
Setting $h=1/n$ yields
$\norm{\emlq_{1/n} - (\cdot)^2}_{\infty,[0,1]} \le \tfrac{4}{9n} = O(1/n)$. For uniform error
$\le\varepsilon$ take $h=\tfrac94\varepsilon$ (equivalently $n\ge\tfrac{4}{9\varepsilon}$).
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
The worst case $2(e-\tfrac52)\approx0.4366$ shows $4/9\approx0.4444$ is nearly tight; the
leading slope is $1/3$. The optimal constant lies in $[\tfrac13,\tfrac49]$.
\end{remark}

\section{A worked numerical example}
Fix $h=\tfrac14$ (i.e. $n=4$): for $x\in[0,1]$, $\emlq_{1/4}(x) = 32(e^{x/4}-1-\tfrac{x}{4})$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:rate} guarantees $\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|\emlq_{1/4}(x)-x^2|\le\tfrac49\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac19\approx0.1111$;
the true worst case (near $x=1$) is $\approx0.0888$. Halving the step provably halves the
certificate. The ratio (error$/h$) decreases monotonically toward the leading slope $1/3$:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{r r r r}
\hline
$n=1/h$ & certificate $\tfrac49 h$ & empirical sup error & ratio error$/h$ \\
\hline
1  & 0.4444 & 0.4366 & 0.4366 \\
2  & 0.2222 & 0.1898 & 0.3795 \\
4  & 0.1111 & 0.0888 & 0.3553 \\
8  & 0.0556 & 0.0430 & 0.3440 \\
16 & 0.0278 & 0.0212 & 0.3386 \\
64 & 0.0069 & 0.0052 & 0.3346 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
This confirms $4/9$ is a valid uniform majorant and that the asymptotically optimal constant is
$1/3$.

\section{Discussion}
Theorems above upgrade existential universal approximation to a constructive statement: an
explicit separating primitive certifies density (even from one generator), and an explicit
exponential increment approximates $x^2$ with the certified constant $4/9$ and $O(1/n)$ rate.
The softplus activation $\log(1+e^x)$ is an EML function, and the strict monotonicity behind
separation is the same property that conditions such activations for gradient training.

\section{Future directions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Uniform Jackson rate for all Lipschitz functions on $[0,1]$:} every
$L$-Lipschitz $f$ admits an EML network of width $O(n)$ with $\norm{f-\text{net}_n}_\infty\le
CL/n$, by superposing shifted exponential increments.
\item \textbf{Sharp constant for the $x^2$ network:} conjecturally the true uniform constant
is asymptotically governed by $x=1$, lying strictly below $4/9$ (slope $1/3$).
\item \textbf{Multivariate monotone separation on $K\subset\R^n$:} coordinatewise separators
$g_i(x)=\log(x_i+1-lo_i)$ separate points of any box, giving density on $\C(K,\R)$.
\item \textbf{Depth-vs-width tradeoff:} one extra $\log\circ\exp$ layer should improve the
$x^k$ rate from $O(1/n)$ to $O(1/n^2)$ by realizing a higher-order finite difference.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}
EML networks admit a clean two-pillar theory: $\log$ supplies a strictly monotone,
point-separating primitive driving Stone--Weierstrass density (even from a single generator
on an interval), and $\exp$ supplies an explicit Taylor-based increment approximating $x^2$
with the certified constant $4/9$ and $O(1/n)$ rate --- a complete small model of
constructive approximation for transcendental network classes.
